# dEQP-GLES2 on the Verdin AM62P — results

How to reproduce any row: `tools/cts/README.md`. Every number here was read off
the board; nothing is estimated, and a row with no measurement says so.

## gl_test's reset_state disabled no attribute array until 2026-09-24

Read this before comparing a gl_test sweep with an earlier one, on any board.

From c8f470de (reset_state) until the commit that renamed gl_context.h's
attribute-array size to `GL_CAP_VERTEX_ATTRIBS` (2026-09-24, M6 step B), every
gl_test run on every board started each case with a failing query.
`src/gl_context.h` defined `GL_MAX_VERTEX_ATTRIBS` as its array size (16), and
`src/gl_internal.h` removed the Khronos token (0x8869) to make room. So
reset_state's `glGetIntegerv(GL_MAX_VERTEX_ATTRIBS, &attribs)` asked for pname
16. That raised GL_INVALID_ENUM ("GL error 0x500 in glGetIntegerv", then
"gl_test: reset_state raised a GL error"). attribs stayed 0, so **no vertex
attribute array was disabled between cases**: an array a case enabled stayed
enabled for the next one. The GL core itself answered 0x8869 correctly; the
fault was the C macro.

After the fix, reset_state disables all 16 arrays, as it was written to. In
the preprocessed gl_test.c for the PowerVR and the GC7000 user builds, exactly
the query's pname changed (16 to 0x8869), plus a static assertion that the
token keeps its value. `tools/check.sh` compiles gl_test.c, so the gate checks
that assertion.

- **The effect on the AM62P and the i.MX8MP is unmeasured.** A sweep before
  the fix and a sweep after it differ in this, not only in what the commits
  between them changed.
- **AM62P case 22 (vao) is expected to change.** Its failure ("reset_state
  raises GL error 0x500 in glGetIntegerv, then default VAO attr0 disabled = 1
  want 0", above) is this defect: attribute 0 was left enabled by an earlier
  case. That is a prediction, not a result, until a board has run it.
- On the Raspberry Pi 4 the error showed before every case of the first
  v3d_gl_test run (4 of 6, STATUS.md section 1b); its two failures are named
  backend refusals, and the rerun after the fix is its own row.

## The wedge rows are pinned to one commit, and cannot be rebuilt at head

Every GC7000 wedge row below -- the ladders, `a_many_temps`, `b_many_instructions`,
the `steps/` rungs -- was measured with the pair built from **`ccb2e8136c4f`**.
That is a requirement, not provenance. At today's head the same sources compile
to something else:

    steps/s20 s24 s28 s32 s36   REFUSED by the temps-21 band ceiling (97e9d00)
    a_many_temps.vert           temps 5, not 44 (the sinking pass, eda47a3)

A ladder rebuilt at head therefore reports a sweep of refusals and a low-temps
arm that draws -- which reads as "nothing wedges" and means nothing. The danger
is not a wrong answer but a confident empty one.

The reverse matters more: **a head-built result neither confirms nor refutes
anything measured on `ccb2e81`**, because the programs are different. Any
head-built arm belongs in its own row, labelled.

`tools/cts/wedge-next-run.sh` checks the tree mechanically -- it names the seven
commits that change what these sources compile to and refuses if any is present
-- so this does not depend on someone having read this paragraph.

## Never edit a script while it is running

`exp2.sh` was running when it was edited to add one line. Bash reads a script
incrementally, by byte offset, so the running shell resumed at an offset that
no longer meant what it had when the file was opened, and died with

    exp2.sh: line 46: unexpected EOF while looking for matching `"'

in a file that is 42 lines long. The line number being past the end of the file
is the signature. Everything after the edit point never ran — in this case the
step that restored the module and the step that resumed the sweep, which is why
the board was left on a probe module afterwards.

Stop it, edit it, restart it. This is the same shape as an install step sharing
a command line with a commit that a hook can refuse: **a multi-step operation
must not be able to lose its later steps without saying so.**

## The texture group's GL_OUT_OF_MEMORY: the pool empties and stays empty

`dEQP-GLES2.functional.texture` returned 27 `ResourceError`, every one
`GL_OUT_OF_MEMORY` on a texture upload. Three explanations were proposed and
all three were wrong before the driver's own line settled it.

    the -EBUSY guard refusing a restarted process   -- refuted: all 27 are GL_OUT_OF_MEMORY
    capacity (the tests upload 2048x2048, 21.3 MiB) -- refuted: the smallest failure is 0.38 MiB
    cube maps unmodelled, so the core returns OOM   -- refuted: 32 of 42 size.cube.* return Fail,
                                                       so they uploaded and rendered

What broke every size-based story is one pair at identical dimensions:

| case | bytes | outcome |
|---|---|---|
| `size.cube.256x256_rgba8888` | 1.50 MiB | ran |
| `size.cube.256x256_l8` | 0.38 MiB | `GL_OUT_OF_MEMORY` |

Four times the bytes, and the larger one succeeds. Failures track **dimension**
— never below 128, mixed at 256 and 512, always at 1024 and 2048 — which is
order- and state-dependent rather than a size limit.

**The driver says why, 94 times in that group's log:**

    render pool exhausted:   132 KiB requested,   80 KiB left
    render pool exhausted:  8196 KiB requested,   80 KiB left
    render pool exhausted: 21848 KiB requested,   80 KiB left

**The pool is down to 80 KiB of ~57.8 MiB and stays there.** So 384 KiB fails
not because it is large but because nothing is left when it asks; the 1.50 MiB
case ran while there was still room. The request sizes name the cases —
21848 KiB is `size.2d.2048x2048_rgba8888_mipmap`.

**What is left to explain** is the gap, not the failure: the close line reports
**22658 KiB reclaimed** at a point where the pool has 80 KiB free, so roughly
35 MiB is accounted neither as live nor as reclaimable. With `dropped=0` ruling
out slot exhaustion, that is a fragmentation or standing-reservation question.

**Two changes landed the same day that target exactly that gap**, and any
re-measurement must account for them rather than read the difference as noise:

- `pvr_render_free` now merges a freed block's neighbours on **both** sides
  rather than the first found. Measured on the host: pool peak fell from 1.41x
  the live peak to 1.27x on a texture-like mix.
- a regrown HWRT tail-pointer or region-header buffer now returns its
  predecessor to the pool instead of dropping it — a real leak, tens of KiB per
  pair per dimension threshold crossed.

Both are in `9d756b9c0ad5` and **in none of the binaries the numbers above were
taken on** (`370d293`, `9a233bb`, `4134cab`). So they cancel within any set of
arms run on one binary, and do **not** cancel against these baselines: a
cross-binary comparison carries two extra variables and the row must say so.

They are also, on their face, candidate fixes for this gap. That makes the
`GL_OUT_OF_MEMORY` count on a re-run a **measurement of them**, not a nuisance
column — and a fall in it is a result rather than noise.

Also worth carrying: `GL_OUT_OF_MEMORY` is **not only a memory error**.
`settle_texture()` turns a fence timeout on a texture still in flight into the
same enum, because ES 2.0 has no other code for "the platform failed". Three
lines tell them apart — `render pool exhausted` (driver, with both numbers),
`render: fence N timeout (<who>)` (driver), and `the kicks using it did not
complete` (client). For this group the first is present 94 times, so it is
memory; elsewhere it may not be.

## The rule the instrument failures all reduce to

**A measurement that could not have observed what it reports is not a
measurement.** Every instrument failure on 2026-09-22 — four of mine and one
of the driver's — was a case of this, and they came from opposite directions:

| direction | example |
|---|---|
| the evidence was destroyed and the number was still printed | an empty dmesg capture counted as `fence = 0`; 19 rows rested on it |
| the join could not have found the record | a +/-3-line window looking for a line that a 123-line dump had pushed out of reach |
| the filter fabricated what it then reported | a `grep` tail making non-adjacent lines look adjacent |
| the thing could not print at all | reporting `MMUCACHE ack not seen` absent without first checking the line exists |
| the code never ran and the number was still believed | 182a80f reverted on a soak whose counters read zero, because the workload could not reach the path |
| an absent field decoded as a real value | `blend_consts_off` missing meant "none", and was read as offset 0 — a valid offset — so the blend colour was written over the first fragment uniform |
| a case that did not exist reported as failing | a sweep invented a `FAIL` for a case number the suite does not contain |

**The shape of the family, named by shaderc-remote: absent-means-something-specific.**
In each case the code had no representation for "this was not there", so it
substituted a value indistinguishable from a real one — 0 for "no log", 0 for
"no blend constants", `FAIL` for "no result". The same hole on three floors of
the stack, found by three people on the same day.

The one that was caught *before* it cost anything belongs in the same table,
because it is the same failure and it shows what catching it early looks like:
a counter that was cumulative since `insmod` would have been read as a
per-run figure under an alternating A/B design, giving a clean-looking
two-hour table whose key column could only increase. It was found by reading
the staged module against the procedure before the slot was spent, rather than
by puzzling over the results afterwards.

The practices that follow, and that this tooling now enforces:

- **Before reporting an absence, establish the thing could have appeared.**
  Grepping and finding nothing is indistinguishable from grepping for something
  that cannot be emitted. Check the source, or check the counter.
- **Report an absent value as absent.** `n/a` when nothing was captured, never
  `0` — because a lost log and a clean run must not look the same.
- **Join on what the instrument actually emits.** The driver stamps
  timestamps, so timestamps are the join key. Line proximity is never one.
- **Never reduce a capture at capture time.** Keep the whole log, in order,
  marked by `/proc/uptime`. Counts can always be derived from a whole log; a
  whole log can never be derived from counts, and the questions that arrive
  later — which wait fired, what preceded the *first* timeout of a session —
  are exactly the ones a tally cannot answer.
- **A number from a workload that cannot reach the code is void**, not weak
  evidence. An A/B arm whose counter shows the path was never entered is
  reported as void rather than as a pass count. (The refusal arm has a second
  case worth separating: a non-zero counter with no refusal taking effect is a
  real result, not a void row.)

## What a run is measured against

Three things decide what a dEQP number means, and all three have to be in the
record or the number is not reproducible:

| | |
|---|---|
| **library pair** | the `.so` files on the board — `GL_RENDERER` and the reported ES version are in the `.qpa`, the commit is not |
| **kernel module** | the driver under them; two modules with the same `lsmod` size can differ in behaviour that changes results |
| **shader server** | the host compiler; a stale one answers everything and quietly measures an older front end |

For the runs below: pair **`8b5428a`**, module **`763c15f`**, server **`24d0e01`**.

*(Corrected: this file briefly said the module was `b607b58` with "182a80f in".
It is not. pvrgpu-platform measured `182a80f` making the board **worse** — 100/100
with 0 fence timeouts on `763c15f` against 96/100 with 28 — and reverted both it
and `9452162` rather than ship a change whose own counters said it never fired.
So the loaded module is `763c15f`, the `-EBUSY` guard alone, and its driver
behaviour is identical to current main's. The absence of an `hwrt busy` line in
dmesg is therefore correct rather than evidence of anything: that counter only
ever existed in the reverted commit.)*

Getting that middle field was harder than it should be. `/sys/module/pvrgpu/version`
does not exist, `dmesg` wraps inside an hour under CTS load and takes the load
line with it, and `lsmod` size plus the `.ko` mtime cannot tell two builds apart.
It was left blank rather than guessed until someone who knew could say. A
`MODULE_VERSION` carrying the commit would make it automatic, which has been
asked for.

### A parameter's description is not the parameter

`modinfo` on the staged probe modules describes `hwrt_cleanup` as cleaning up
"the HWRTDatas **and freelists**". The binary does not touch the freelists: that
half was written and then removed, because the DDK's `RGXDestroyHWRTData_aux`
only decrements each freelist's refcount and `RGXFWRequestFreeListCleanUp` has
one caller in a separate lifetime — and ours are module-wide, shared by every
live dataset, so a recycle releasing them would pull three lists out from under
fifteen datasets. The code was fixed and the description was not.

Worth recording because it is the exception to the rule the rest of this file
argues for. "Read it from the artefact" is right for the **version** and the
**parameter values**, which the module computes: `/sys/module/<dev>/version` is
`MODULE_VERSION`, and `/sys/module/<dev>/parameters/*` are the live variables.
It is wrong for a parameter's **description**, which is a string a human wrote
and nothing checks against the code. A stale one survives every rebuild.

So a row quotes the version and the values from sysfs, and quotes a parameter's
meaning from the source that implements it — never from `modinfo`.

The module was deliberately **not** restaged for the text: one binary under two
names in a queue is worse than one stale sentence that is known about.

### The module version in a row is checkable

A row's module column is the string the board reported in
`/sys/module/pvrgpu/version`, and that string is the first twelve characters
of a commit hash. It is worth stating that the hash resolves, because for part
of 2026-09-22 it did not: the modules being measured were built from commits
that existed only in their author's worktree, so rows were faithfully
recording a version nobody else could look up. They were merged (not rebased,
which would have renamed them and orphaned every row) and the chain now closes:

```sh
$ git rev-parse 370d293 | cut -c1-12      # what the rows cite
370d293a0da8
$ git merge-base --is-ancestor 370d293 origin/main && echo ok
ok
```

Both halves matter and neither substitutes for the other. Reading the version
from sysfs is what stops a filename standing in for a module — a staged `.ko`
has twice been superseded by a newer build under a similar name, and once
reported `-dirty` while its filename claimed a clean commit. Checking the hash
is an ancestor of `origin/main` is what stops the recorded version being
unresolvable. A row that cannot be traced to a public commit is not a
measurement anybody else can repeat.

## The hardware clips z the D3D way — measured, 2026-09-22

The near/far question that `clip_neg_z` raised is answered. pvrgpu-platform built
`z_probe` (links `libyakogl.a`, so the backend option stays out of the shipped
`.so`) and drove all three clip modes:

| depth-clip mode | z = −0.5 | z = +0.5 | z = +2.5 | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 (none) | drawn | drawn | drawn | nothing clips |
| 1 (`FRONT_REAR`) | **clipped** | drawn | clipped | **`0 <= z <= w`, the D3D convention** |
| 2 (`FRONT_REAR_DEPTH`) | drawn | drawn | drawn | nothing clips |

z = −0.5 is inside GL's `-w <= z <= w` volume and outside a `0..w` one, so it is
the discriminating case; z = +2.5 is the control both conventions clip.

**That verdict was over-generalised, and the correction matters more than the
original.** It varied the clip *mode* and held `CR_PPP_CTRL` at `0x202`. Varying
both shows the hardware does either volume, and `0x202` was simply asking for the
wrong one — it inherited Mesa's Vulkan value:

| `ppp_ctrl` | depth-clip | z = −0.5 | z = +0.5 | z = +2.5 | volume |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `0x202` | 1 | **CLIPPED** | drawn | CLIPPED | D3D, `0 <= z <= w` |
| `0x203` | 1 | **drawn** | drawn | CLIPPED | **GL, `-w <= z <= w`** |

z = −0.5 is inside GL's volume and outside a `0..w` one, so it discriminates;
z = +2.5 is the control both conventions clip, and it stays clipped at `0x203`,
which proves the clipper is running rather than switched off.

So **bit 0 of `CR_PPP_CTRL` is the clip-volume switch**, gles2-core's reading of
the DDK capture was right, and the near/far fix is **one constant** — not a
coordinate remap in every vertex shader and every entry of the offline table.
That is the difference between a one-line change and a rebuild of the shader
table, decided by seconds of board time.

The lesson is the day's recurring one: the first probe held a variable fixed and
the conclusion was drawn as though it had not. Mode 2 (`FRONT_REAR_DEPTH`) still
clips nothing at all at either `ppp_ctrl`.

That is `clip_neg_z`'s "diamond missing from the centre" explained exactly, and
it is why the depth clip is off by default (`680365d`) rather than left on.

| group | cases | pass | fail | notsup | crash | noexec | fence |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `info` | 6 | **6** | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| `prerequisite` | 3 | **3** | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| `negative_api` | 246 | **237** | **0** | 9 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| `state_query` | 396 | **395** | **1** | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| **total** | **651** | **641** | **1** | **9** | 0 | 0 | 0 |

Against the same 651 cases earlier the same day: 526 pass on the first
GPU-backed pair, 603 on `cca781a`, **641 now**. `negative_api` went 94 failures →

The single survivor is `state_query.shader.program_active_uniform_types`
(`got invalid value`), which gles2-core had already flagged as reflection rather

**This is the `uniformTestVertSource` prediction landing.** Eighteen of the 24

## The stall is a missing MMU cache acknowledgement — measured, 2026-09-22

The fence timeouts that have been costing whole groups are caused by the
driver not waiting for the firmware to acknowledge the pre-kick MMU cache
invalidate. `mmu_cache_sync()` lost that wait; the probe module `370d293a0da8`
puts it back behind a parameter, so it can be turned on and off on one boot.

One module, one boot, one variable. Parameters read back from
`/sys/module/pvrgpu/parameters/` after each load, never echoed from the
command line; version from `/sys/module/pvrgpu/version`. Workload
`./hwrt_thrash 5 4` from the `es2-8b5428a` pair.

| combined_kick | mmu_ack | mmu_gate | fence timeouts | workload |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| N | Y | Y | 4 | completed 16 sizes |
| N | Y | N | 9 | completed 16 sizes |
| Y | Y | Y | **0** | completed 16 sizes |
| N | N | Y | never reached | **wedged**, no output in 400 s |
| Y | N | Y | 18 | completed 16 sizes |

Two single-variable comparisons carry it. With the combined kick held fixed,
`mmu_ack` on gives 0 timeouts and off gives 18. With the two-kick path held
fixed, on gives 4 and off never produces a single render. `mmu_gate` runs the
other way from intuition: invalidating on every kick (gate=0, 9) is worse than
invalidating only when a mapping changed (gate=1, 4).

A dEQP group agrees, which matters because the reproducer cannot report
success (below). `dEQP-GLES2.functional.flush_finish`, the group that carried
5 fence timeouts in the sweep:

| module | cases | pass | fail | warn | noexec | fence |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| the sweep's row, old module | 5 | 2 | 0 | 0 | 3 | 5 |
| `370d293a0da8`, ack=1 gate=1 comb=1 | 5 | 3 | 0 | 2 | 0 | 1 |

All five now return a result and none fails; the two warnings are
`CompatibilityWarning`, allowed in a mustpass run. The three cases that never
executed now do.

### What this measurement does not say

- **`hwrt_thrash` fails its colour check in every arrangement, including the
  one with no timeouts**, and the first reading of that here was wrong. It was
  written up as "wrong pixels", as if renders were completing against stale
  data. `0000ffff` is the **clear colour**: `hwrt_thrash.c` sets
  `glClearColor(0, 0, 1, 1)` immediately before the clear. So every one of those
  readbacks is the clear landing and the draw never appearing — a different
  fault, and one much closer to the stall family than to staleness. The six
  `GL error 0x502` from `current_drawable_program` say the same thing from the
  other end: an INVALID_OPERATION raised client-side, before any GPU work
  exists, means some draws were never issued at all. A stale TLB does not
  explain that, so it is not evidence for the MMU story and is not counted as
  such. Only the fence counts were used from this reproducer.
- **The board rebooted before these rows** (uptime 35 s, the stock `pvrsrvkm`
  had reclaimed the GPU). None of this shares a boot with the earlier
  "firmware exactly one kick behind" captures. All five rows above do share
  one boot with each other, which is what the comparisons need.
- `370d293` is a **probe module, not a shipped fix**. The fix is restoring the
  wait in `mmu_cache_sync()`. A row measured against a probe names no commit.

### Which caller emits the residual timeout

Four callers share the one `render: fence N timeout` message — the frame
fence, an HWRT member busy (`:687`), an HWRT recycle (`:718`), and the
geometry UFO throttle (`:982`). Two of them log a line of their own after the
wait returns and only when it failed, so a companion identifies its caller.

**Attribute by timestamp, never by line proximity**, and this section exists
mostly to say so. `dump_last_frag_cmd()` runs between the timeout line and the
caller's own line and prints over a hundred lines. A first pass here used a
+/-3-line window and reported "0 of 27 are HWRT waits" — from a capture that
held a companion **123 lines** below its own timeout, 0.97 s later. The window
looked obviously generous and could not have contained the answer. The
companion's return code matters too: `-110` (ETIMEDOUT) is a wait that timed
out and printed the timeout line; `-5` (EIO) is the HWR bail, which returns
without printing it and must not be matched to a timeout.

Corrected, over the same 27 timeouts (`tools/cts/cts-timeouts.py`):

| attribution | count |
|---|---|
| HWRT member busy (`:687`), companion `rc=-110` 0.97 s later | 1 |
| `no free HWRT slot` (`:718`) | 0 — the line never appears |
| no companion, no label: frame fence **or** the silent `:982` | 26 |

So the HWRT member-busy wait **does** fire and is not excluded. Only `:718` is
excluded on real evidence. The remaining 26 cannot be attributed from an
unlabelled log at all, because the two candidates are both silent. The probe
module `f5431cf04d75` names the wait in the message, which is how this is
answered rather than inferred.

Two further facts from the same 27, both robust to the above:

- **Every one has `ufo` exactly one behind `fence`** — 27 of 27, including
  those taken with the acknowledgement wait on. The one-kick-behind invariant
  survives in the residual.
- They carry only **17 distinct fence numbers**, so counting message lines
  overstates the number of stalls by about a third.

And a related absence, scoped: `render: MMUCACHE ack not seen` appears **zero**
times across a window containing all 27 timeouts. The line exists
(`pvr_render.c:961`) and was checked to exist before its absence was reported.
The unambiguous case is the `flush_finish` run that showed a residual timeout
while `mmu_ack=1`: the firmware acknowledged inside 100 ms and the render still
stalled, so the wait is not silently failing and the residual is a different
mechanism.

### The origin: every stall begins one wait-period after an HWRT recycle

Captured on `9a233bbb938d` with the acknowledgement wait at its default, the
labelled build, one client, `hwrt_thrash 5 4`. **The log itself is committed**,
at `tools/cts/captures/arm0-dmesg-full.txt` — whole ring, in order, unfiltered,
with `captures/README.md` giving the module, parameters, workload and window.
Evidence for a finding this size does not belong in a gitignored build
directory.

**The session recovers repeatedly — one stall per frame, not one render
repeated.** 31 timeout lines are 15 distinct episodes (each fence times out
twice, 20 s apart); `ufo` advances 75 → 187, so **112 renders retired**; between
episodes fence and `ufo` advance together by 4 to 32. Every timeout is labelled
`waiting on the frame fence`; **not one is `:687`**. That is a different animal
from the unrecovering 386-second cascade above, which did contain a `:687`.

At the first timeout of the session:

    [4472.023566] HWRT pair 4 (48x33) recycled for 288x162
    [4472.123235] HWRT 288x162 x1 ...                  <- last driver activity
    [4492.139934] fence 76 timeout (ufo=75) waiting on the frame fence
    [4492.259523] stall: geom rd=8400 fw_w=8400 host=8512 |
                         frag rd=30000 fw_w=30000 host=30400 | KCCB rd=108 w=108

`fw_w == rd` on both rings and `host` ahead by exactly one kick (112 geom, 400
frag): the firmware consumed everything it read and never took the last kick.
`KCCB rd == w`, so the command path is not backed up.

**The correlation, and the base-rate test that the naive version fails.**
Recycles occur every ~19 s, so a random instant has one within 20 s with
probability **0.515** — "15 of 15 within 30 s" is worthless. What is not base
rate is the tightness:

| | |
|---|---|
| gap from recycle to an episode's first timeout | min 20.02 s, max 20.12 s |
| P(a random instant's gap falls in 19.8–20.4 s) | 0.014 |
| observed | 15 of 15 |
| chance of that by coincidence | 1.9e-28 |

The gap equals the wait period to within 0.1 s every time, so **the wait that
expires began at the moment of the recycle**: the render submitted onto a
just-recycled pair is the one that fails to retire.

**The converse holds too, once recycles are grouped.** The 31 recycle *lines*
are **15 bursts** (a gap of more than 1 s starts a new one; sizes 1,1,1,1,1,1,
1,1,1,2,2,2,3,5,8 — several pairs are recycled within milliseconds when the
working set turns over). Against the 15 episodes:

| | |
|---|---|
| bursts followed by an episode | **15 of 15** |
| episodes preceded by a burst | **15 of 15** |
| bursts with no episode | **0** |

So the correspondence is **one to one**, and the earlier framing here — "31
recycles produced 15 episodes, so the converse is not established" — was an
artefact of counting lines instead of events. There is no population of
recycles that did not stall, and therefore no question of what distinguishes
them.

The last recycle of each burst is the one the 20.02 s gap is measured from, in
every case.

**This is not the `:687` amplifier.** The recycle path *succeeds* here — it logs
`recycled for`, not `no free HWRT slot` — so `:718` never times out and the
reuse counter stays 0. That is also why `hwrt_refuse` could not be exercised.

### Three stall shapes, told apart by the walker and the freelist line

Every stall prints the same `fence N timeout`, and three different failures
hide behind it. They are separated by the driver's own walker line — where the
firmware's read pointer sits against what it has taken (`fw_w`) and what the
host posted — and by the freelist line.

| | shape 1 (recycle) | shape 2 (stopped geometry DM) | shape 3 (kick never taken) |
|---|---|---|---|
| seen in | `hwrt_thrash`, arm 0 | `functional.texture` (the sweep) | the 386 s cascade |
| geom | `rd == fw_w`, host +1 kick | **`rd < fw_w == host`** | `rd == fw_w == host` |
| frag | `rd == fw_w`, host +1 kick | `rd < fw_w == host` | **`rd=0, fw_w=0, host=800`** |
| freelist | `pending=0` | **`pending=1`** | `pending=0` |
| recovers | yes, 112 renders retired | no | no |
| recycle nearby | yes, 15 of 15 | **none at all** | — |
| reading | the firmware has not taken the last kick | it has taken the work and is not running it | it never took the work, though both fences read `MET` |

**The freelist line is what separates 2 from 3**, and it was the question that
produced it:

    shape 2   freelist1 cur=512 top=511 max=4096 grow=256 ready=0 pending=1 alloc=0
    shape 3   freelist1 cur=512 top=511 max=4096 grow=256 ready=0 pending=0 alloc=0/0

Shape 3's pending-command walk says the work was ready when the firmware
ignored it:

    frag[0] off=0   FENCE ufo 0xc00d3584 needs 1, is 1  (MET - the firmware should be running this)
    geom ccb has nothing unread

So a fix for one shape is not a fix for another, and **a clean run of one
workload says nothing about the shapes it cannot produce**. `hwrt_thrash`
recycles constantly and produces shape 1; the texture group never recycles
(the HWRT cache is per module and survives dEQP's restarts) and produces
shape 2.

### A second stall shape, with no recycle anywhere near it

The recycle correspondence above was measured inside one workload. A real dEQP
group shows a different shape, and it is the one costing cases.

Captured while the sweep was in `dEQP-GLES2.functional.texture` on
`370d293a0da8`, one client (`tools/cts/captures/texture-group-ring.txt`):

| | `hwrt_thrash 5 4` | `functional.texture` |
|---|---|---|
| fence timeouts | 31 | 51 |
| distinct `ufo` values | many, advancing 75 → 187 | **1** — frozen at 1711 |
| lag (`fence - ufo`) | always exactly 1 | grows 1 → 31 |
| recovers between stalls | yes, 112 renders retired | **no** |
| `recycled for` lines | 31 | **0** |
| `render: HWRT ` setup lines | 127 | **0** |

**The absence of recycle lines is real, not a logging artefact**, and that was
checked rather than assumed: `370d293`'s source contains both lines at
`LOG_INF`, identical to `9a233bb`; and the same ring carries 18
`pvrgpu: close:` lines, which are also `LOG_INF`, so INFO reaches it.

The explanation is that **the HWRT cache is per module, not per client**
(`ensure_render`), so it survives dEQP's crash-restarts — 48 of them in this
group. Once populated with the sizes a group uses there are no misses, no
creations and nothing to recycle, while `hwrt_thrash` cycles 24 sizes against
16 pairs and recycles constantly.

This does not refute the 15/15, which stands within its workload. It means the
recycle is **not the only origin**, and not the origin of the stalls that cost
conformance results: this group carries 27 `ResourceError` and 21 `Timeout`,
each costing a process restart. **A fix that corrects the recycle path may
leave this shape untouched**, and a clean `hwrt_thrash` after such a fix must
not be read as the stall being solved.

### The four-arm recycle run, and a withdrawn caveat worth keeping

The follow-up run varies `hwrt_cleanup` x `hwrt_reinit` (0/0 today, 1/0
handshake only, 0/1 re-init only, 1/1 both) on `pvrgpu-probe-10c8449.ko`
(`10c844912ebd`), which supersedes `a2f161d` and `aca053a`.

**A rule was recorded here saying the `sub`/`exec` column is void on any arm
with `hwrt_reinit=1`, and it is withdrawn.** The concern was that the parameter
zeroes the dataset's `cleanup_state`, so the counts would read equal because we
wiped them rather than because the firmware had finished. On this module that
cannot happen — verified in the file, not from the discussion:

| `driver/src/pvr_render.c` | |
|---|---|
| 872, 878 | `HWRT recycle: ... cleanup sub/exec=%u/%u` — **unguarded by any arm parameter** |
| 888 | `if (pvr_render_hwrt_cleanup)` — the handshake |
| 929 | `recycled for` |
| 1017-1018 | `if (pvr_render_hwrt_reinit)` then the `memset` |

The counters are printed as the firmware left them, at every recycle, on every
arm, before anything touches them. The column is comparable across all four.

**The category the caveat named is real even though this instance was not**, so
it stays on the record: *an instrument under test manufacturing the evidence for
its own hypothesis*. That is distinct from the absence-substituted-by-a-value
family above — nothing is missing, the measurement is simply produced by the
code whose behaviour is in question. It is why the arms have to be read against
where each parameter acts, rather than uniformly.

One module revision **was** withdrawn for a real reason: `a2f161d`'s arm 1
posted CLEANUP/FREELIST alongside the HWRTData cleanup. The DDK does not —
`RGXDestroyHWRTData_aux` only decrements each freelist's refcount, and freelists
outlive the datasets that point at them. Ours would have been worse than the
DDK's, because **three freelists are shared by all sixteen pairs**: every
recycle would have asked the firmware to release memory fifteen other live
datasets still referenced, and a worse-than-baseline arm would have read as a
real measurement of the handshake.

### The HWRT member-busy wait proceeds, and the session never recovers

`:687` waits for the HWRT pair member still in flight, logs `still busy at
seq`, and then does `return pick;` — handing the set out while the kick that
owns it may still be reading its region headers. Whether that matters was
answerable from a capture already in hand, by ordering rather than adjacency:

    ts=1446.375   fence timeout                  <- the :687 wait's own timeout
    ts=1447.340   ":687 still busy ... (-110)"   <- times out, proceeds anyway
    ts=1468.751   fence timeout   (+21.410 s)
    ts=1488.871   fence timeout   (+20.121 s)
        ... 18 more, every 20.120-20.122 s without exception ...
    ts=1832.030   fence timeout
    ts=1832.133   client closes

**Twenty further timeouts follow the proceed, in the same client session, and
the run never recovers** — it ends only when the client gives up, 386 s later.
The spacing is the tell: 20.12 s to within 2 ms, twenty times running, is a
wait period expiring rather than work failing at random. After the proceed,
every render waits its full timeout and gets nothing.

**The period does not identify the caller**, and is easy to misread as if it
did. Three of the four waits use the same 20000 ms — verified in source:

| wait | timeout |
|---|---|
| `:691` HWRT member in flight | 20000 ms |
| `:722` HWRT pair recycle | 2000 ms |
| `:986` geometry UFO ring throttle | 20000 ms |
| frame fence (`WAIT_MS`, `src/pvr/backend.rs`) | 20000 ms |
| chardev close drain (`pvr_chardev.c:199`) | 1000 ms |

So a 20.12 s cadence says "a timeout is expiring" and nothing more. Only
`:722` is separable by period, and it is independently excluded.

The **last** event in the cascade is identified by its period, though: `+1.106 s`
rather than 20.12 s, and 1000 ms is the only one-second wait in the driver —
the chardev's close-time drain. So the session was still wedged at the moment
it closed, which is what the cascade implies and this confirms independently.

What this does and does not establish:

- It **propagates**. This is not one event absorbing itself.
- It may **amplify rather than originate**. The `:687` wait timed out because
  the member had not completed, so a render was already stuck before `:687`
  said anything. Proceeding may be what turns a stalled render into a wedged
  session.
- The twenty have no companion, so each is a frame fence or the silent `:982`
  — undecidable from an unlabelled log, and unaffected by that: whichever they
  are, they are downstream in time.
- The capture's other two sessions have no `:687` event and show three
  timeouts each rather than a cascade. Consistent, not conclusive.

### A fence count of zero that was a lost log

Nineteen rows of the first mustpass sweep printed a fence count that rested on
no evidence. The board-side capture marked its position in the kernel log with
a line count and then took the tail from there — and the ring buffer wraps
within the hour under CTS load, which is exactly what a line-count mark cannot
survive: the buffer stops growing monotonically, the tail runs off the end,
and the capture comes back **empty**. An empty capture was then counted as
**zero fence timeouts**.

A group whose evidence was lost was therefore indistinguishable from a group
where the GPU behaved, in the one column this investigation turns on. It was
caught because the board's own ring still held timeouts at timestamps falling
inside groups the table called clean.

The mark is now a timestamp from `/proc/uptime`, which a wrap cannot
invalidate, and a group with no captured log reports `n/a`. This is the same
rule the `reuse`/`evict` columns already followed and it should have been
applied here first: **an absent value is absent, never zero.**

### A zero that meant nothing

The first attempt at the `flush_finish` comparator returned **0 fence
timeouts**, and that number was worthless: all five cases had failed at shader
compile, because the reboot lost `YAKOGL_SHADERC_SERVER` and the board fell
back to `127.0.0.1:7777`. Zero timeouts because zero work reached the GPU. The
run is kept as `flushfinish-NO-SHADER-SERVER`. Any run reporting a suspiciously
clean driver number should be checked for transport markers before it is
believed — `cts-summary.py` flags them above the failures for this reason.

## The pair under 4d81c9f wrote the blend colour over a fragment uniform

Every sweep row on the pair `es2-8b5428a` was measured with a library that
zeroed the first fragment uniform of every fragment shader.

The remote shader back end decoded an absent `blend_consts_off` as **0** — a
real offset, where a block's first uniform sits — where "no blend constants"
is the sentinel 255, and the server omits the field for every shader that has
none. So the draw path wrote `glBlendColor` over the application's first
fragment uniform, which then read (0,0,0,0).

    fix  4d81c9f  2026-09-22 09:15   "an absent blend_consts_off is the sentinel"
    pair 8b5428a  2026-09-22 06:55   the sweep pair -- predates it

The defect is in `src/shaderc/remote.rs`, so it is compiled into the pair
rather than being something the compile server could correct underneath a run.

**Measured on the GC7000: 6 of 38 gl_test cases** (24/38 → 30/38 with the fix).
**Not measured on the PowerVR.** `remote.rs` is GPU-agnostic and the server
omits the field identically, so the same clobber is expected there — but that
is an inference, and it is recorded as one until the head-pair re-run settles
it.

What it does to the rows: any case whose fragment shader reads a uniform at
dword 0 may be an artefact rather than a failure, and the signature is "a
value that should not be zero came out zero". Structural failures — attribute
aliasing, relink holes, `max_*` limits, preprocessor cases, crashes — are not
explained by a zeroed uniform and stand. The failure list is not wrong about
*what* failed; the library underneath a share of it is in question.

This is why the post-sweep head pair is built from `4d81c9f` or later rather
than from the earlier commit originally specified: one re-run then answers
this at the same time as the clear, clipping-z, `uniform_api`, `light_amount`
and `shaders.struct` predictions.

### A stall with no pool exhaustion anywhere in its window — 2026-09-22

The `texture`-group evidence above has exhaustion 150.6 s **before** the first
fence timeout, which rules out the stall having emptied the pool and leaves the
reverse open. This is the counterexample to the reverse: **a stall with no
`render pool exhausted` line at all.**

Measured on `370d293a0da8` with the sweep's parameters (`do_boot=1 mmu_ack=1
mmu_gate=1 combined_kick=1`), during a head-pair re-run of the 683 failing
cases, one client. Counted from the module's own load line so that nothing
before the reload is mixed in:

| after the reload at board clock 16737.43 | count |
|---|---|
| `render pool exhausted` | **0** |
| `render: fence N timeout` | 5, first at 18415.57 |
| `recycled for` | 0 |
| hardware recovery | 0 |

So pool exhaustion is **not necessary** for the stall. Together with the
`texture` ordering, which says the stall does not cause the exhaustion, the
pool and the stall are not in a simple causal line in either direction, and a
pool fix cannot be assumed to move this.

The stall line is a third signature, and the difference from the frozen-`ufo`
shape above is in the KCCB rather than the walker:

    stall: geom rd=24752 fw_w=24864 host=24864 | frag rd=17600 fw_w=18000
           host=18000 | KCCB rd=93 w=93 | gufo[seq 1098]=1097

Both rings have the firmware behind the host, and **the KCCB is fully drained**
(`rd == w`), where the wedge captured in `wedge-370d293-15871.txt` had a
backlog of 17 commands (`rd=17 w=34`). `ufo` froze at 1097 across five
timeouts, as it froze at 1711 there.

One caution about reading `dmesg` for this: the ring holds both wedges, and
the two `pool exhausted` lines in it (board clock 16572.9) belong to the
earlier one, 165 s BEFORE the reload. Counting them into this window is the
easy mistake and it inverts the conclusion.

## Which run supersedes which

These numbers were taken against three different libraries in one day, and they
**replace** each other rather than accumulating. Reading them together would be
wrong:

| library | what it is | status |
|---|---|---|
| `b295183 + 90b4ef3` | first GPU-backed pair; reports **ES 3.0**, so dEQP applies ES 3.0 rules | superseded |
| `8be6150` | first `YAKOGL_REPORT_ES2=ON` pair | superseded: predates `c90dcf4` (near/far clipping) and `e54f5dd` (state_query fixes) |
| `cca781a` | ES2 + remote shaderc + the clipping and state_query work | **current** |

So the 603/651 from `8be6150` measures a build without the near/far clipper, and
the `cca781a` sweep replaces it. Do not add them together or quote the better of
the two.

242 of 256 shaders that dEQP invented at run time compiled, linked, ran and gave
the right answer. **No case failed for a transport reason** — the summary's
"shader compiler was not reachable" check did not fire once, so all 14 failures
are real results about the shader toolchain, not about the server being down.

What it was run against:

- **Library**: the Rust YakoGL userspace pair in `~torizon/yakogl-user` on the

- **Driver**: `pvrgpu.ko` from driver `00e5320`, `do_boot=1`, freshly reloaded.
- **Config**: `rgba8888d24s8ms0`, pbuffer, 256x256, `YAKOGL_LOG=0`.
- **Version reported**: this pair was built *without* `-DYAKOGL_REPORT_ES2=ON`, so

  rules whatever the version string says. Three rules belong to ES 2.0 alone and are
  gated on that option — `glUniformMatrix*fv` with `transpose = GL_TRUE`,
  `glGenerateMipmap` of an NPOT texture, and NPOT completeness — so some
  `negative_api` expectations here are the ES 3.0 ones. Rows taken against a
  REPORT_ES2 build are labelled as such.
- **Shader server**: up (yakogl `671c6a9`) but **not exercised** — none of these
  four groups compiles a shader dEQP invents, which is why they were chosen to go
  first.

`info` and `prerequisite` are clean. The other two are API-semantics groups that
need no rendering, so every number here is about the GL state machine, not about
pixels.

### Where the 116 failures are

By the message dEQP recorded:

| reason | count |
|---|---|
| `Got invalid error` | 84 |
| `Failed to retrieve uniform location` | 10 |
| `got invalid value` | 7 |
| `Got invalid float value` | 6 |
| `Failed to compile shader` | 6 |
| `expected GL_TRUE` | 3 |

`Got invalid error` dominates, and it means one thing: the call was supposed to
set a specific `glGetError` code for an illegal argument, and set a different one
(or none). That is the error-checking half of the GL entry points, and it is
mechanical to fix — each case names the exact call and the code it wanted.

`negative_api`'s 94 failures concentrate in `texture` (52) and `shader` (25), then
`state` (9), `vertex_array` (6), `buffer` (2). `state_query`'s 22 are almost all in
`shader.*`, split between `Failed to compile shader` and `got invalid value`.

The full list, one case per line with its reason, is in the run's
`failures.txt`; regenerate it for any run with
`cts-summary.py --failures-file`.

### The 14 shader failures

They fall into exactly two groups, and neither is a YakoGL runtime problem.

**12 of 14 are a matrix vertex attribute** —
`shaders.functions.datatypes.{,float_}mat{2,3,4}_{vertex,fragment}`, i.e. every
matrix width in both stages, and nothing else in `datatypes`. All twelve carry the
same message, character for character:

```
glsl2usc: pco_shc failed for shader.vert:
pco_shc: ../src/imagination/pco/pco_nir_pvfio.c:909: lower_pvi: Assertion `attrib' failed.
```

`shaderc-remote` narrowed it against the same `pco_shc`, and it is **not** matrices
as function arguments, which was this file's first and wrong reading: a matrix as a
function argument compiles, and so does a matrix *varying*. A matrix **attribute**
is the whole failure — it spans N consecutive attribute locations and `pco_shc`'s
per-vertex-input lowering asserts on it. Writing it as N `vec<rows>` inputs and
reassembling with `mat2(c0, c1)` compiles cleanly, so the fix belongs in the
ES 1.00 -> GLSL 450 rewrite (`tools/yakogl-tools/src/glsl.rs`), not in `pco_shc`
and not in the transport.

(How this file got it wrong the first time is worth keeping: the message is two
lines, and it was read with a line-based grep that saw only the first, so the
reason looked blank and was reported as a second bug in the log pass-through.
There was no such bug. `cts-summary.py --logs-file` now writes every failing
case's logs out whole, which is how this should have been read.)

**2 of 14 are missing validation**, and they fail the other way round:
`functions.invalid.argument_basetype_mismatch_fragment` and
`functions.invalid.return_array_in_struct_fragment` say *"expected compilation to
fail, but shaders compiled correctly"*. The front end accepts two constructs
GLSL ES 1.00 forbids.

### Reading this honestly

526 of 651 is not a conformance number and must not be quoted as one. It is four
groups out of thirty, chosen because they are the ones that work without the
run-time shader path. Adding `shaders.functions` makes it 768 of 907 across five
groups — still not a conformance number. `shaders` alone is 10101 cases, of which
this is 256, and everything that draws a pixel is still unmeasured: `fragment_ops`
(1923), `uniform_api` (1267), `texture` (807), `fbo` (709), `clipping` (602),
`vertex_arrays` (571).

## What the shader groups should do, before any board time

`tools/es100_oracle.py --codegen` runs dEQP's own `data/gles2/shaders/*.test`
cases through the whole pipeline — the ES 1.00 front end, the rewrite to GLSL
450, glslang and `pco_shc` — on the host, in minutes and with no GPU. Measured
here at `455ff02`:

    TOTAL   2793 cases   2785 met   8 missed   99.7%

and independently by es100-frontend at `094016b`: the same 2785/2793, the same
eight. `pco_shc` refuses nothing the front end accepts, so in
`conditionals`, `constants`, `conversions`, `declarations`, `fragdata`,
`functions`, `keywords`, `linkage`, `loops`, `misc`, `qualification_order`,
`reserved_operators`, `swizzles` and most of `preprocessor`, **a compiler abort
on the board is news rather than the expected state**.

The eight known misses, so they are not re-reported as discoveries:

| case | why |
|---|---|
| `preprocessor.basic.identifier_with_double_underscore` (×2) | glslang rejects consecutive underscores below `#version 300`; GLSL ES 1.00 allows them |
| `preprocessor.predefined_macros.file` (×2) | filename-based `__FILE__` needs `GL_GOOGLE_cpp_style_line_directive` |
| `preprocessor.conditional_inclusion.basic_2` (×2) | glslang refuses `defined` expanded from a macro |
| `scoping.valid.local_variable_hides_function_parameter` (×2) | GLSL ES lets a local shadow a parameter; the GLSL 4.50 we rewrite into calls it a redefinition |

**What this does not answer.** The oracle scores compile and link verdicts only,
never rendered values, so a case it calls `pass` can still draw the wrong thing.
And three of the largest groups have no `.test` file for it to read, because dEQP
generates them at run time: `operator` (2949), `random` (1898) and `matrix` (738).
Those 5585 cases can only ever be answered on silicon, and they are where board
time is worth spending.
