### A counting bug in my own summary, caught before it was sent

The first version of that file's header said case 2 had **29** wrong checks. It
has four. The counter matched every line carrying `want`, and a *passing* check
prints `want` too — so 25 passes were counted as failures, and the
nothing-drawn classification was computed from the same bad set (it said 10
cases, not 14). Counting only lines that also say `MISMATCH` fixes both. A
summary that miscounts in the direction of "more broken" is the kind that gets
quoted.

## The refusal histogram's biggest bucket is a hole in a sentence

The lead asked for a per-construct breakdown under the top four reasons, on the
basis that the front end carries the construct in the error's token. It does
compute it — `lower.rs:725` passes `other.kind_name()`, `Error` is
`{ line, tok, msg }`, and `mod.rs:47` documents the rendering as glslang's own
shape, `0:5: 'x' : message`.

**The token never reaches the info log.** `codegen.rs:349`:

    lower::compile_to_ir(scratch, st, src)
        .map_err(|e| CompileError::Rejected { line: e.line, msg: e.msg })?;

`CompileError::Rejected` is `{ line: u32, msg: &'static str }`. There is no
token field, so `e.tok` is discarded one call before it could be logged. What
the board emits, 1,841 times byte-identical, is

    0:0: assignment to this is not lowered yet

with a gap in the sentence where the construct belongs. That is why 1,869
distinct constructs collapse into the largest bucket on the work list, and why
the bucket cannot be split from any log.

Checked against the raw `.qpa` text before being reported, because
`cts-refusals.py` stops its match at `<` and truncation had to be ruled out
first. It was not truncation; the string on the wire carries no token.

Two smaller findings from the same look: every message reads `0:0:`, because
several `Error::new` calls pass a literal zero for the line (`lower.rs` 120,
573, 697, 725), so a rejection cannot be located in the source either. And
`codegen.rs:529` asserts a rejection always has a message — the assertion that
would have caught this is the one nobody wrote, on the token.

### What was not done, deliberately

The breakdown could have been faked convincingly. dEQP's case names carry the
construct — `conditionals.if.*`, `conversions.scalar_to_vector.*`,
`indexing.uniform_array.*` — so bucketing 1,869 case names by prefix would
have produced a table that looks exactly like a per-construct histogram.

It would have been a measurement of the test suite's naming, not of the
compiler, and nobody reading it later could have told the difference. A number
that cannot be traced to the thing it claims to measure is worse than an
absence, because an absence gets fixed. The gap was reported instead, with the
one-line location; the histogram regenerates itself the moment the token is
carried, since the documented format is the one the extractor already parses.

## The remote control sweep wedged the GPU, and the wedge message was wrong

The remote-pair control over the same 11,376 cases got **1,434 cases in**
(Pass 1017, Fail 400, QualityWarning 10, NotSupported 3) and then the GPU
wedged. The three-strikes detector fired correctly: pass 0 died at 1,431 cases
with status 137, then three consecutive passes each died after **one** case.

**The wedge is real, and it was checked rather than assumed** — because 137 has
a second explanation that would have been mine, not the board's: if the shader
server on 7779 had died, every compile would hang, the runner's watchdog would
kill dEQP, and it would look exactly like this. So both were tested:

    7779 still listening                     yes (pid unchanged)
    es100_triangle on the board              opens /dev/gcgpu, then HANGS
                                             exit 124 after 120 s
    the board's own log                      12 events in flight,
                                             fences 25341..25352 unsignalled

So: the GPU, not the harness. Clearing it needs a module reload, which needs
sudo, which this session does not have on either board.

### Two defects in my own wedge message, both fired on their first real use

    == the GPU is wedged: the known VDM/tiler stall, which only a
    ==   ssh torizon@<imx8mp> 'sudo rmmod pvrgpu && sudo insmod gles2 '

1. **It named the AM62P's mechanism as fact on a Vivante board.** The VDM/tiler
   context-store stall is a PowerVR thing. This is a GC7000. The runner had
   measured "nothing completes" and printed a cause it could not know.
2. **The recovery command was wrong twice in one line.** `pvrgpu` is the other
   board's module — this one is `gcgpu` — and `$BOARD_MODULE` is *dEQP's*
   module name (`gles2`), not a kernel module, so it told the reader to
   `insmod gles2`, which is not a driver and does not exist as a file.

A recovery instruction that cannot work is worse than none: it costs a confused
attempt before anyone doubts it. The message now states only what was measured
(no draw completes), says to read the board's own log for which stall it is,
and builds the command from `BOARD_GPU_DEV`, which is the variable that
actually names the GPU module.

Both were invisible until the wedge happened on the second board. The first
board's wording was right, so nothing looked wrong for as long as there was
only one board — which is the ordinary way a hard-coded assumption survives.

## The new message format broke the extractor, and the fixture caught it

es100-frontend's `fc88b41` makes the online compiler print glslang's shape:

    0:59: '.' : assignment to this is not lowered yet

and said the extractor should parse it unchanged. **It did not.** Fed that
format, `cts-refusals.py` returned every reason as the *empty string* — three
fixture cases collapsed into one nameless bucket, and nothing in the output
said anything was wrong.

The cause is one character. dEQP writes the info log XML-escaped, so the quotes
around the token arrive as `&apos;`, and the pattern excluded `&` from the
message so it would stop at an entity. That was correct while the message had
no token and silently captured nothing the moment one appeared, because
`&apos;` begins immediately after the colon.

**The board is wedged, so this cost nothing.** Had it not been, the rerun would
have spent forty minutes producing a histogram of one nameless row — a result
that looks like a measurement, since "9,244 refusals" would still have been
right. The tool was checked against the new format *before* the run because the
run was impossible, which is luck; the rule it should have followed anyway is
the one already in this file for rungs: **an instrument that has never been fed
the new input is not yet evidence about it.**

Fixed: unescape the entities first, then parse `0:<line>: '<tok>' : <msg>` into
its three parts. The token then gives the per-construct split for free — the
thing that could not be produced at all this morning:

    2  assignment to this is not lowered yet
           1  .
           1  []

`tools/cts/testdata/refusals-new-format.qpa` pins it, and
`cts-selftest.sh` check 16 asserts all three: the message is named, a case dEQP
marked `Pass` stays out of the work list, and one message over two tokens
splits by construct. The last is the one that fails if the token is ever lost
again.

Unescaping also corrected the old run's own numbers: reasons went from 73 to
87 distinct, because messages that contained an entity had been truncated at it
all along. The gap total is unchanged at 8,417 in 24 reasons — the truncated
ones were all in the correct-refusal set.

## M5's board procedure, and a kexec defect the second board would have hit

`gc-milestone.sh m5` boots the Zephyr `gc_gl_test` image — built with the online
compiler and no shader table — through the kexec crash route and reads the
result off the panel and the hold time. Written and dry-run while the GPU is
wedged; nothing in it has met silicon.

What it refuses, tested rather than asserted:

    no M5_IMAGE                     refuses, names the variable
    M5_IMAGE that is not readable   refuses, names the path

What it puts in the row, because an M5 claim without these is not a claim: the
image's sha256 and build time, and **the Kconfig read back from the build's own
generated `.config`** — `CONFIG_YAKOGL_SHADERC_ONLINE` and
`CONFIG_YAKOGL_NO_SHADER_TABLE` especially. An image that still links the
offline table is not an M5 image, and the only honest way to know which it is
is the `.config`, not the command line someone remembers typing. If the
`.config` is missing the row says so in those words rather than omitting the
line.

The verdict comes from the hold time, with the plan document's arithmetic —
kernel start = (now − jump) − `/proc/uptime`, so a slow boot is not read as a
long hold — and 55–75 s reads PASS, 35–50 s FAIL, **anything else UNREADABLE**
with an instruction to read the panel rather than a guess.

### The kexec defect

`kexec_run.sh` unloaded `pvrgpu` and `pvrsrvkm` before the jump — **the AM62P's
modules, both of them**. On the i.MX8MP the driver holding the GPU is `gcgpu`,
so the jump would have left our own module loaded and owning the hardware while
Zephyr came up, and nothing in the output would have said so: `rmmod` of an
absent module is silenced, and the ssh session ends at the jump either way.

It is the same shape as the wedge message that named the AM62P's stall, and the
same shape as `cts-run.sh` documenting the AM62P as `BOARD_HOST`'s default: a
single-board assumption, invisible while there was one board, wrong the moment
there were two. Three of them in one day, all in the same runner, all found
only by using the second board.

Now `BOARD_GPU_MODULES`, defaulting to all four (`pvrgpu pvrsrvkm gcgpu
galcore`) so an operator who sets nothing gets the old behaviour plus the
Vivante one. Unloading a module that is not loaded is free; not unloading one
that is costs the boot.

### A quoting failure worth one line

The first draft computed the verdict with an `awk` program inside `"..."`
inside `$( )`, and a `cut -d" "` inside a single-quoted ssh command inside the
same. Both closed the outer string early and `bash -n` reported the error
**forty lines below** the real one. The fix is not cleverer quoting: it is not
nesting three levels of it. The verdict is plain shell now, and the uptime is
read with `awk '{print $1}'`.

## The fence-timeout recovery works, and the A/B says so within one session

`gcgpu` `469e79b2f91d` (srcversion `2C902D2BD67B490124D380A`, sha256
`51b2556040cc...`), loaded through `sudo -n /usr/local/sbin/gcgpu-reload`.
Online pair `gc4-es100online-469e79b2f91d`.

The A/B precondition pvrgpu-platform set -- *arm A must wedge in the same
session or the measurement is VOID* -- is **met**: arm A wedged.

It did not need a 40-minute sweep, because the trigger turned out to be
deterministic and at the head of the list. `shaders.algorithm` is the first
subgroup of the shaders caselist alphabetically, and the online sweep died in
it twice: pass 0 after `hsl_to_rgb_vertex`, pass 1 after `rgb_to_hsl_vertex`,
then pass 2 ran the remaining 10,093 cases without trouble. So the whole A/B is
those four cases. `build/cts/ab-algorithm.txt`, `build/msg/ab-recover.sh` and
`build/msg/ab-armB.sh`.

`GPU_RECOVER` is unset in **both** arms, so `cts-run.sh` never reloads the
module: the only recovery in play is the driver's own, and the arms differ by
`recover_off` alone.

| | arm A `recover_off=1` | arm B (default) |
|---|---|---|
| `hsl_to_rgb_fragment` | Fail | Fail |
| `hsl_to_rgb_vertex` | Timeout | Timeout |
| `rgb_to_hsl_fragment` | **Timeout** | **Fail** |
| `rgb_to_hsl_vertex` | Timeout | Timeout |
| fence timeouts / recoveries | 3 / 0 | 2 / 2 |
| GPU after the run | **dead** | **alive** (`es100_triangle: PASS`) |

Two things separate the arms, and the second is the one that matters.

**The GPU never comes back in arm A.** Every timeout there reports `completed
1`: fence 2 wedged and fences 3 and 4 were issued into a GPU that had stopped,
so the in-flight list grew (`event 0`, then `0,1`, then `0,1,2`) and the three
later cases timed out as collateral. In arm B the second timeout reports
`completed 3` -- fence 3 *ran and finished* after the first recovery. That line
is the mechanism, not just the outcome: the reset restores the GPU, it does not
merely unblock the waiter.

**One case got its real verdict back.** `rgb_to_hsl_fragment` is a Timeout in
arm A and a `Fail` in arm B -- the same `Fail` the full sweep recorded. A wedge
does not only lose the case that caused it; it corrupts the verdict of every
case behind it until someone reloads the module. That is the cost the recovery
removes, and it is why the earlier sweep needed three passes for `shaders`
while this one needed the same three but finished.

The completed sweep ran the **online** pair `gc4-es100online-469e79b2f91d`
(our own compiler, in-process), not the remote one -- worth stating beside the
numbers, because the same figures from the remote pair would mean the reference
compiler's baseline rather than ours: `shaders Passed: 874/10097`,
`uniform_api 239/1267`, `attribute_location 31/57`.

### The safety condition pvrgpu-platform named did not occur

> a "recovering the GPU" line in dmesg and the same case reported PASS

Both abandoned fences map to a case reported **Timeout**, never Pass:

    recovering the GPU (fence timeout): fences 2..2 abandoned, 1 already done   -> hsl_to_rgb_vertex  Timeout
    recovering the GPU (fence timeout): fences 4..4 abandoned, 3 already done   -> rgb_to_hsl_vertex  Timeout

Same in the full sweep (fences 116 and 118, the same two `*_vertex` cases).
No abandoned kick was reported as a pass, so `fence_lost()` is doing its job.

### The instrument that would have hidden all of this, fixed and then exercised

The previous run reported **"no GPU fence timeouts and no recoveries during
this run"** while the kernel log held 13 timeouts and 2 recoveries. The pattern
was `render: fence [0-9]+ timeout`, which is `pvrgpu`'s wording; `gcgpu` writes
`fence N did not complete in`. A false clean, on the one line a reader trusts
to tell them the numbers above are sound. It now matches both drivers and
counts `recovering the GPU` separately.

This A/B is its first real exercise, and both arms came out right: arm A
`3 GPU fence timeout(s) and 0 GPU recovery(ies)`, arm B `2 ... and 2 ...`.
An instrument that has never been fed the new input is not yet evidence about
it -- the rule this file already states for rungs -- so it is worth saying that
this one has now been fed both.

### A bounded wait can still hold the module: the reload race

Arm A's reload of the module for arm B failed with `rmmod: ERROR: Module gcgpu
is in use`, and `/proc/*/fd` named no holder. The kernel's own counters did:
`refcnt=1`, and `ps` showed `es100_triangle` in state **D**.

`gcgpu_release()` takes `cd.lock` and then waits up to 1000 ms for the last
fence -- deliberately bounded, and deliberately not cut short by a signal, so
that memory going back to the pool is not still being read by the GPU. The
consequence is that for up to a second after the probe is killed the module is
still in use, and `timeout -k 5` cannot shorten it: `SIGKILL` does not reap a
task in `D`. Nothing was wedged; the reload was simply early, and the process
was gone on the next look.

Arm B waits for `/sys/module/gcgpu/refcnt` to reach 0 before reloading, reading
the kernel's count rather than guessing at a sleep. This is the same lesson as
`pgrep -f`: ask the kernel what is true, do not infer it.

## The GPU is wedged by what OUR compiler emits, not by the workload

The same four cases, the same driver module (srcversion `2C902D2BD67B490124D380A`,
reloaded before each run), the same GPU, `recover_off` at its default:

| pair | shaders from | result | timeouts / recoveries |
|---|---|---|---|
| `gc4-es100online-469e79b2f91d` | **our online compiler** | Fail, Timeout, Fail, Timeout | 2 / 2 |
| `gc3-remote-0ed4cc64cc89` | the reference compiler | **Pass, Pass, Pass, Pass** | **0 / 0** |

The remote pair's kernel log is empty: not a recovered wedge, no wedge. And all
four cases *pass*, so the hardware renders this workload correctly when it is
given a correct program.

The prediction was written before the run (`build/msg/ab-remote-control.sh`) and
it is the one that held: the wedge follows the shader back end.

**The source has no loop.** `hsl_to_rgb` and `rgb_to_hsl` are a 6-arm
`if / else if` chain over `sextant` with no iteration of any kind
(`es2fShaderAlgorithmTests.cpp:173`). So "a shader that never terminates"
cannot be true of the GLSL. It can still be true of what we emit -- and the
back end's open item is exactly branch targets on `SelInstr`. A branch that
lands on the wrong target makes a loop where the source has none, and the GC7000
then runs it forever: `IDLE_STATE` with FE, PE and SH busy, which is what every
dump of this wedge has shown.

### The internal control, which needs no second build

Within the online pair itself, on one pair, one hash, one driver, one case
family: the two `*_fragment` variants **do not wedge** and the two `*_vertex`
variants **always do** -- in the full sweep (fences 116 and 118), in arm A and
in arm B. The only thing that differs between `hsl_to_rgb_fragment` and
`hsl_to_rgb_vertex` is which stage the expression is compiled into. That
excludes the GL core, the driver and the case's GL state, and leaves the emitted
shader.

The cross-pair comparison does carry one confound worth naming: `gc3` and `gc4`
are different YakoGL commits, so strictly the remote row differs by pair as well
as by back end. The clean version is a remote pair staged at `469e79b2f91d`, or
an online pair at `0ed4cc64cc89`; neither is staged today. The internal control
above is what makes the conclusion hold without it.

### Why this matters beyond a failing case

This is a compiler defect of a class the others are not: it does not draw the
wrong picture, it **hangs the GPU**. On this board a module reload or the new
fence-timeout recovery clears it. In the product image there is no module to
reload. Before `shaderc-online` ships in a Zephyr image, a non-terminating
program has to be impossible by construction or bounded by the hardware, not
recovered after the fact.

### Two instrument notes from this run

`gc4-es100offline-469e79b2f91d` was tried as a same-hash control and the pair
guard **refused it**, correctly: an offline pair has no run-time shader back end
and dEQP writes its shaders as it runs, so every case would have failed to
compile and the table would have looked like a result. The guard did its job.

Deriving the offline script from the remote one with `sed` rewrote the results
directory but not the log path, so the offline run overwrote
`build/msg/ab-remote.log`. The remote verdicts survived only because the script
was run under `tee` into `ab-remote.out`. Deriving a script by substitution
edits the paths you thought of; `tee` kept the evidence.

## Correcting myself: there is ONE minimal trigger, not two, and a second shape

I reported both `*_vertex` cases as triggers. Run alone, on a freshly loaded
module, only one of them is:

| case, run ALONE on a fresh module | verdict | recoveries | runs |
|---|---|---|---|
| `hsl_to_rgb_vertex` | **Timeout** | **1** | 2/2 |
| `rgb_to_hsl_vertex` | Fail | 0 | 3/3 |
| `hsl_to_rgb_fragment` | Fail | 0 | 1/1 |

This file already warned that *the case named at a wedge is where the process
died, not what wedged it*, and I had repeated the mistake it warns about --
`rgb_to_hsl_vertex` was named at a wedge in the sweep, in arm A and in arm B,
and is not a trigger on its own. The check that caught it costs one minute.

**The minimal reproducer is one case and one shader:**
`dEQP-GLES2.functional.shaders.algorithm.hsl_to_rgb_vertex`, online pair, fresh
module. `tools/cts/testdata/wedge-shaders/` holds its exact GLSL.

### Shape 2: a wedge that needs a previous kick, and that a reset prevents

`rgb_to_hsl_vertex` is not harmless -- it wedges reproducibly, but only with
something in front of it:

| sequence | second case | recoveries | runs |
|---|---|---|---|
| alone | Fail | 0 | 3/3 |
| after `rgb_to_hsl_fragment` | **Timeout** | 1 | 2/2 |
| after `hsl_to_rgb_fragment` | **Timeout** | 1 | 1/1 |
| after `hsl_to_rgb_vertex` (which wedges, then the GPU is **reset**) | Fail | 0 | 1/1 |

Both of my predictions for this were wrong, which is why it is worth writing
down. A prior *recovery* does not make it wedge -- it **prevents** it. A prior
ordinary kick does. So the GPU that has just been reset behaves like a fresh
one, and the thing that matters is whether another kick has been placed before
this one.

### Not pool reuse, and not stale contents: the knobs refute it

The obvious story is memory the previous kick left behind, and the driver
already has the knobs to test it. Prediction written first: if it is reuse,
`pool_no_reuse=1` turns that Timeout into a Fail.

| module args | second case | recoveries |
|---|---|---|
| `pool_no_reuse=1` | Timeout | 1 |
| `scrub_allocs=1` | Timeout | 1 |
| defaults | Timeout | 1 |

**Refuted, both of them.** Not the allocator reusing a block, and not the
contents of the block. So the knobs should not be tuned further here.

What survives is that the wedge depends on *where the program is placed*, not
on what is in the memory around it -- a fresh pool puts the shader at one
address, a pool with a previous allocation in it at another, and a reset
returns it to the first. **A branch target that is position-dependent behaves
exactly like this**: correct at the offset it was built for, and a jump into
whatever follows at any other. That is the same defect already suspected from
`hsl_to_rgb_vertex`, seen from a second angle, and it makes the emitted
branch's addressing the thing to read rather than the pool.

I cannot close it from the board: confirming it needs the emitted code
disassembled at both placements, which is the compiler team's side of the seam.

Pairs built and staged today from `origin/main` `ccb2e8136c4f`, which contains

| pair | result | failing |
|---|---|---|
| `gc5-es100online-ccb2e8136c4f` (our compiler) | **25 of 29** | 9 stencil, 16 msaa, 20 etc, 61 texincomp |
| `gc5-es100offline-ccb2e8136c4f` (blob table) | **25 of 29** | 9 stencil, 16 msaa, 20 etc, 61 texincomp |

**The two are identical, case for case.** The online path was 5 of 29 before
this fix. Our own compiler now produces the same gl_test verdicts as the
offline table, and the four that remain fail on *both* paths -- so they are not

### Every one of the 20, as asked, not only the 13 predicted

| group | cases | outcome |
|---|---|---|
| predicted flips (gles2-core) | 2 3 4 5 6 8 10 11 12 13 14 22 23 | **13/13 PASS** |
| negative control, must not regress | 1 18 24 34 60 | **5/5 still PASS** |
| **unpredicted** | **19** | **PASS -- it flipped** |

Two of these need saying plainly rather than folding into the count.

Recorded as its own line because a 14-for-13 result would otherwise quietly
