## The wedge is not our compiler's alone, and the temps ceiling is not the rule

Two hypotheses were on file for `hsl_to_rgb_vertex` hanging the GC7000: a 6-bit
`NUM_TEMPS` wrap (67 & 0x3f = 3), and the `vs_load_balancing` band's temp
ceiling. One pair built at `ccb2e81` (pre-refusal: `3d15144`, `6905b7c`,
`262db8b`, `35df4ac`, `b8b3cb1` all verified absent), recovery on, a fresh
module load per arm, dEQP's grid of 92.

| arm | pair | temps | outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| `hsl_to_rgb_vertex` | online | 67 | **WEDGE** |
| `hsl_to_rgb_vertex` | remote | 10 | PASS |
| `a_many_temps` | online | 44 | **WEDGE** |
| `a_many_temps` | **remote** | **40** | **WEDGE** |
| `b_many_instructions` | online | 5 | PASS |
| `b_many_instructions` | remote | 2 | PASS |

**The reference compiler's output hangs the GPU too** (`a_many_temps`, temps
40). So this is not "our compiler emits something bad", which is how I reported
it earlier in the day and is corrected here: our allocator *reaches* the
condition sooner (67 temps where the reference uses 10), but the reference gets
there on its own as soon as a shader needs enough registers. The defect is on
the driver side of the seam.

The wrap is **refuted**: 44 and 40 both hang and neither crosses 0x3f. A bound
of 63 -- in the allocator or at the driver seam -- admits every hanging case in
this table.

### The boundary, and why it is not a temps ceiling either

Walking one shader shape (K live `vec4`s summed into one varying, no control
flow) across the range:

| temps | 12 | 16 | 20 | 24 | 25 | 26 | **27** | 28 | 32 | 44 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| | PASS | PASS | PASS | PASS | PASS | PASS | **WEDGE** | WEDGE | WEDGE | WEDGE |

Sharp and reproducible at **26 -> 27** for that shape. But it is not a rule
about temps, and the counter-example is one of the original shaders:

    k23.vert              temps 27,  ~69 instructions   WEDGE
    rgb_to_hsl_vertex     temps 28,   95 instructions   PASS

Measured through the **same instrument, same session**, so this is not two
harnesses disagreeing. A shader with *more* temps and *more* instructions
passes where a smaller one hangs. Whatever selects the bad state is correlated
with register count and is not determined by it, so a ceiling -- 21, 26 or 63 --
is a mitigation with an arbitrary constant, not the fix. The number the driver's
load-balancing formula has to reproduce is not a single threshold.

This also dissolves the "placement" story for `rgb_to_hsl_vertex` rather than
confirming it: at temps 28 it sits just past where this shape breaks, it passes
alone, and it needs another kick in front of it to go over. Marginal, not
positional -- which is why `pool_no_reuse` and `scrub_allocs` changed nothing.

### The instrument, because three versions of it were wrong

`es100_vsprobe` takes a vertex shader, a fragment shader and a grid size. Each
of the first three versions reported a clean PASS on a shader that provably
hangs the GPU under dEQP:

1. A constant-colour fragment shader never read the varying, so the vertex work
   was dead code and was optimised away. **The program measured an empty shader
   and printed PASS.**
2. No `a_unitCoords`, so the shader ran on `(0,0,0,1)` -- in `hsl_to_rgb` that
   makes `(v - m) / v` into 0/0, data the case never sees under dEQP.
3. One quad: 6 vertex invocations where dEQP's `GRID_SIZE` 92
   (`glsShaderRenderCase.cpp:61`) runs 8,649.

Only after the third fix did it reproduce the known wedge, and nothing it said
before that counted. A first results table also called three remote arms
"WEDGED" because no PASS line was printed -- while the kernel log showed **zero**
fence timeouts. They were compile refusals, from a fragment shader of mine
missing `precision mediump float;`. A wedge cannot be silent in the kernel log,
and the verdict rule now separates refusal, wrong picture, hang and other.

That refusal is a finding of its own: **our online front end accepted a
fragment shader that glslang rejects** -- `float` with no default precision
qualifier. A false accept, for es100-frontend.

### The bisect stops: the two pairs disagree at the same temps

pvrgpu-platform set the stop condition themselves -- *"if the two pairs ever
disagree at the same temps count, stop; that is a different finding and worth
more than the bisect"*. They do, at temps 27, back to back, twice each:

| shader | pair | temps | instr | outcome |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `k23` | **online** | **27** | 69 | **WEDGE** (2/2) |
| `k27` | **remote** | **27** | 52 | **PASS** (2/2) |

And within our own compiler the outcome is **not monotone in temps** either:

| `k22` | online | 26 | 66 | PASS |
| `k23` | online | 27 | 69 | **WEDGE** |
| `rgb_to_hsl_vertex` | online | **28** | 95 | **PASS** |

More registers *and* more instructions, and it runs. So a rule of the form
"refuse above N temps" is not merely a mitigation with an arbitrary constant --
it is the wrong **shape** of rule, and no bisect on temps can produce the number
pvrgpu-platform is waiting to substitute for their 21.

Everything measured so far, in one place:

| shader | pair | temps | instr | outcome |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `b_many_instructions` | online | 5 | 212 | PASS |
| `b_many_instructions` | remote | 2 | 50 | PASS |
| `hsl_to_rgb_vertex` | remote | 10 | 48 | PASS |
| ladder 12..26 | online | 12-26 | 24-66 | PASS |
| `k23` | online | 27 | 69 | **WEDGE** |
| `k25`..`k28` | remote | 25-28 | 48-54 | PASS |
| `rgb_to_hsl_vertex` | online | 28 | 95 | PASS |
| ladder 28..44 | online | 28-44 | 72-120 | **WEDGE** |
| `a_many_temps` | remote | 40 | 78 | **WEDGE** |
| `hsl_to_rgb_vertex` | online | 67 | 220 | **WEDGE** |

Register pressure is clearly involved -- every wedging arm is register-heavy and
every arm below temps 27 passes on both compilers -- but it does not decide the
outcome on its own, and the counter-examples are not marginal cases needing a
prior kick: they are clean, repeated results on a fresh module.

**My own prediction here was wrong.** I wrote, before the run, that if the limit
were a hardware property the remote pair would break at the same 26 -> 27. It
did not. That is recorded rather than quietly dropped, because the whole value
of the remote arm is that it can disagree.

### One check worth the ten minutes it cost

The temps in every table above were first measured by compiling on the host at
my worktree HEAD, while the board pair is `ccb2e81`, and `git diff` showed
**172 changed lines in `alloc.rs`** between them. A temp count from the wrong
compiler would have mislabelled every row. Re-measured in a worktree pinned to
`ccb2e81` (`build/wt-ccb2e81`): identical, every rung and every shader, so the
labels stand. The check was cheap and the alternative was a table that looked
right and was not -- the same failure mode as the paraphrased shader that cost
gles2-core a refutation.

### The boundary moves with num_out: the bound and the band are related

pvrgpu-platform's experiment, in place of a bisect they were right to stop:
run the same ladder shape at a second `num_out`. Same instrument, same pair
(`ccb2e81`), same grid, fresh module per arm; K live `vec4`s summed into **four**
varyings instead of one, with a fragment shader that reads all four (a varying
nothing reads is dead, and the vertex work with it).

| num_out | band word | last PASS | first WEDGE |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `0x0f3f0241` | temps **26** | temps **27** |
| 4 | `0x0f3f0316` | temps **28** | temps **29** |

    num_out 4:  t23 PASS   t25 PASS   t27 PASS   t28 PASS | t29 WEDGE   t31 WEDGE

**It moved.** Temps 27 and 28 both hang in the one-varying band and both draw in
the four-varying band, on the same compiler and the same silicon. So the limit
is a function of the band, which is what pvrgpu-platform needs to fit the
formula's A and B from structure rather than from a curve through my points.

### And it is still not the whole rule

Two facts from the earlier tables survive this and must be carried with it:

| shader | num_out | pair | temps | outcome |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `k23` | 1 | online | 27 | **WEDGE** |
| `k27` | 1 | remote | 27 | PASS |
| `rgb_to_hsl_vertex` | 1 | online | 28 | PASS |

Same band, same temps, different outcomes -- across compilers (27) and within
one compiler (27 wedges, 28 draws). So `temps <= f(num_out)` is necessary-looking
but not sufficient: something in the emitted code still selects the bad state.
The band relation is real and fittable; a guard built only from it will still
admit `k23`.

Also: `rgb_to_hsl_vertex` declares `varying mediump vec3` where the ladder uses
`vec4`. Whether the band is keyed on varying *count* or on components is not
settled by anything measured here, and it is the obvious next thing to vary if
the fit does not come out clean.

### What the board cannot answer yet

`VS_LOAD_BALANCING` (0x0830) read back on a wedging and a drawing arm is the one
assumption nobody has checked -- that the hardware sees the word we programmed.
There is no path to it: `gcgpu_uapi.h` exposes INFO, ALLOC, FREE, MAP_PHYS,
SUBMIT, WAIT and COMPLETED, and no register read. It needs a driver change, not
a harness change.

## The board rebooted under the register read-back, and galcore took the GPU back

Building pvrgpu-platform's read-back module (`d3be989`) first needed the board's
**own** kernel tree. The one on this host is 6.6.138-7.6.1; the board runs
6.6.142-7.7.0, so the first build came out with the wrong vermagic and `insmod`
would have refused it. `modinfo` says so before the board does -- worth checking
there rather than on the board:

    built here   vermagic: 6.6.138-7.6.1 ...
    board        6.6.142-7.7.0

The 6.6.142 tree had been in `/tmp` and was wiped. It now lives in
`build/imx8mp-ktree/` (fetched from `/usr/src/linux.tar.bz2` on the board,
`modules_prepare` with `LOCALVERSION=-7.7.0`, which is not optional), which is
also the leftover of the pool task. Rebuilt against it: `vermagic 6.6.142-7.7.0`,
`version d3be989d4245`, and it loaded.

**Then the first wedging arm rebooted the board.** `k23`, temps 27 -- the arm
that had wedged and recovered many times earlier the same day. uptime 1 min,
boot at 08:50. There is no pstore on this board, so no panic text survived.

**Not claimed as causation.** One event, no crash log. What is true is that the
only thing that changed is a module whose stall dump now reads shader-state
registers, and that reading registers from a hung GPU is a plausible way to hang
the bus into a watchdog reset. It could equally be coincidence. Confirming it
means deliberately crashing a board with no remote reset, which is not a call to
make alone, so it is asked rather than done.

### What the reboot exposed, and it stops all board work

On boot, **`galcore` -- the vendor Vivante driver -- auto-loads and takes the
GPU**: refcount 5, `/dev/galcore` present. `gcgpu` then loads and cannot bind.
The tell is that `lsmod` shows it with refcount 0, `/dev/gcgpu` does not exist,
and **dmesg contains no `gcgpu` line at all** -- not a failure message, nothing,
because the probe never ran.

`rmmod galcore` is outside the scoped NOPASSWD rule (`gcgpu-reload`,
`rmmod gcgpu`, `dmesg`), so the board needs one command from someone with root:

    sudo rmmod galcore

Worth making durable rather than repeating every reboot: blacklist `galcore`,
and add `rmmod galcore` to `/etc/sudoers.d/gcgpu`.

The known-good module (`469e79b2f91d`) was put back at
`/home/torizon/gcgpu/gcgpu.ko` so the next reload brings up a driver we trust;
the read-back build is parked beside it as `gcgpu-d3be989-readback.ko`, out of
the load path.

### And the measurement it was built for is DELETED -- do not rebuild it

> **`dump_regs` and `dump_after_submit` no longer exist** (`72b5fd6`). The
> paragraphs below are kept because they record how the hazard was found, not
> because the knobs are available. **Reading the shader-state registers from
> the CPU resets this board**, on a busy GPU and on one that has just answered:
> two builds, two reboots, against zero in dozens of runs without a read-back
> build. Anyone reaching this section for "how do I take a reading" should stop
> here -- the answer is that you cannot, and rebuilding the knob ends in a third
> reboot. The HI/PM/MC dump (`hi:`, `pm:`, `mc:`) is untouched and is what
> closed the clock-gating candidate.
>
> Corroboration from pvrgpu-platform, needing no board: the kernel etnaviv
> driver reads 35 distinct registers across its whole file and **not one is at
> or above 0x800**; its debugfs dump is the same set. The vendor does not read
> the state space from the CPU either.
>
> If a state reading is ever needed again, the shape that never touches the
> register file from the CPU is a `LOAD_STATE` read-back into a buffer the CPU
> then reads. Parked, not forgotten.

What follows is the reasoning as it stood at the time.

`dump_regs` dumped **immediately on write**, and the sysfs node was mode 0200, so
triggering it needed root. A wedging arm got the dump free from the stall path;
the **drawing** arm -- which is the comparison -- could not be reached at all from
inside the scoped rule. A load-time parameter fixed that without any new
privilege, because `gcgpu-reload` passes its arguments to `insmod`. That
parameter is what took the board down the second time.

### Board fact: ONE Zephyr run per boot, unless the holder is stopped first

Beside the standing hazard below (every reboot hands the GPU to `galcore`) sits
its consequence for Zephyr work, measured on 2026-09-22:

**A Zephyr run ends in an SoC reset, the board reboots, `docker-compose.service`
starts the product with it, and the product holds `galcore`.** The next
`kexec-zephyr` then cannot `rmmod` a module in use, and the jump does not
happen. So a sequence of M5 arms is not a sequence: the first runs, and every
one after it needs the holder stopped again.

That is what voided the offline EC control. The standing procedure until the
user's A/B decision says otherwise is: stop the holder before every jump.

Two changes make the void impossible to misread rather than merely unlikely:

1. `gc-milestone.sh m5` **refuses before the jump** if anything holds
   `galcore`, reading `/sys/module/galcore/refcnt` and naming the containers:

        galcore     : refcnt 5, containers: sarta
        verdict     : REFUSED to jump -- galcore refcnt is 5

   and exits 3 without booting anything. The point is not tidiness. A negative
   hold (-36.1 s) was obvious; a *positive* number from a jump that never
   happened would not have been, and that is the reading this prevents.

2. The row records whether the board **rebooted since the last arm**, from the
   boot time it already reads, so a VOID is classified where it happened
   instead of being reconstructed from two timings afterwards:

        rebooted    : YES since the last arm (was 2026-09-22 10:40:00)

Both were exercised offline against a stubbed `ssh` and an invalid host -- the
refusal path, the pass-through at refcount 0, and all three states of the
reboot column -- because testing a jump guard by letting it jump would have
destroyed the fault record this board is currently holding.

### galcore is a standing hazard, and the wrapper now says so

The reboot exposed a trap worth more than the incident: **every reboot of this
board silently hands the GPU to the vendor driver.** `galcore` auto-loads, takes
the device, and `gcgpu` then loads *without binding* -- `lsmod` shows it at
refcount 0, `/dev/gcgpu` never appears, and **dmesg carries no `gcgpu` line at
all**, because the probe never ran. There is no error anywhere; it presents as
"no GPU work runs" with no cause attached.

The fix is team-lead's and goes further than the refusal I first wrote: the
wrapper **removes galcore itself** when it is loaded (it already runs as root
through the rule), the sudoers rule gains `rmmod galcore` for the manual form,
and `--blacklist-galcore` is an opt-in that stops it loading at boot. After one
re-run of the setup script, a plain `sudo -n gcgpu-reload` brings the board back
from any reboot with nobody's help. My version only refused and said what to do,
which still needed a human every time; theirs was the better answer and mine was
dropped rather than merged, because both edit the same lines.

### The read-back, second attempt: staged and not yet run

pvrgpu-platform removed the register reads from the fence-timeout path and added
the load-time parameter (`5f1b0dc`), so the drawing arm is reachable inside the
scoped rule:

    sudo -n /usr/local/sbin/gcgpu-reload dump_after_submit=1

Built against `build/imx8mp-ktree/linux` (`vermagic 6.6.142-7.7.0`,
`version 5f1b0dc01495`, and `modinfo` confirms the parameter is present) and
staged as `/home/torizon/gcgpu/gcgpu.ko`, with `469e79b2f91d` kept beside it as
`gcgpu-469e79b2f91d-known-good.ko` and the suspect build as
`gcgpu-d3be989-readback.ko`. Nothing is loaded and nothing is measured: the
board is still blocked on `rmmod galcore`.

**The confirmation run is not being done**, on pvrgpu-platform's judgement about
their own change: one event with no panic text is not a finding, the fix costs
nothing, and it removes the hazard whether or not the module caused it. Buying
certainty would cost a reboot of a board with no remote reset.

## M5: a recovered wedge can no longer read as a clean PASS

The driver recovers a wedged GPU by resetting it, which costs a frame. On a
cluster that is safety-relevant, so an M5 verdict has to say it happened -- and
the panel channel cannot show a kernel log, which is where the recovery line
lives.

`gc_sample_verdict()` now reads the driver's counter itself and **overrides the
sample's own result**: a run with `gc_render_resets() != 0` reports
`FAIL the GPU was reset during the run`, plus the count, however well its own
checks went. `gc_sample_finish()` encodes it in the hold time when no sample has
claimed a code -- 56 + (N - 1), N clamped at 8, so the return time alone says
"recovered N times".

The sample does not have to remember to call anything. `gc_render_resets()` is
declared `__weak` in `gc_sample.c` returning 0, so a sample that does not link
the Vivante driver still builds; when the driver *is* linked its own definition
wins and the count arrives automatically. The hazard being guarded is a
recovered hang read as success, and a guard a sample can forget to arm is no
guard.

**Checked, because a weak symbol that quietly wins is exactly this class of
silent failure.** Built into the real Zephyr image
(`gc_gl_test`, `verdin_imx8mp/mimx8ml8/a53`, `CONFIG_YAKOGL_SHADERC_ONLINE=y`,
with the `-DBOARD_ROOT` that `env.sh` does not set), then read the symbols
rather than trusting the build:

    zephyr.elf                  T gc_render_resets     (one definition)
    vivante/gc_render.c.obj     T gc_render_resets     <- the real counter
    gc_common/gc_sample.c.obj   W gc_render_resets     <- the stub, overridden

Had the stub won, the counter would have read 0 forever and the guard would
have passed every run while reporting nothing.

## The vendor-stack control: present, but not runnable headless

With galcore holding the GPU, the vendor stack could in principle answer the one
question this investigation has never had a control for -- does the VENDOR
driver draw the ladder rungs that hang ours? The answer today is "cannot run",
and the reason matters, because "the vendor stack is not on the board" would be
wrong.

**It is there.** `torizon-qt6-yocto:arm64-imx8` and `sarta-demo:local` (both
already pulled; nothing was fetched) carry the real Vivante user space:

    /usr/lib/libEGL.so.1.5.0   /usr/lib/libGLESv2.so.2.0.0
    /usr/lib/libGAL.so         /usr/lib/libVSC.so

`es100_vsprobe` links against it correctly -- the loader picks the vendor
`libGLESv2.so.2` (it warns "no version information available", which is how we
know it is not ours; no library of ours was placed beside the binary, so
`$ORIGIN` finds nothing and the container's `/usr/lib` wins).

**What stops it is the display, not the GPU.** Both images ship a
**Wayland-only** EGL:

    EGL: Warning: No default display support on wayland
    es100_vsprobe: eglInitialize failed

`EGL_PLATFORM=fb`, `surfaceless` and `x11` all give the identical warning, so the
selector is not consulted -- the build has one backend. `strings` on
`libEGL.so.1.5.0` lists `wayland` and nothing else. And there is no compositor
to talk to: no `/run/user/*/wayland-*`, no weston process, and the one running
container (`sarta`) has no `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR` and no socket of its own.

So the run needs either an fbdev/surfaceless build of the vendor EGL or a
compositor image, and both mean pulling something. **Stopped here as instructed
rather than installing anything.** If the user wants this control, pulling a
`weston-vivante` image (or any image with a non-Wayland Vivante EGL) is the
whole cost, and the probe and shaders are already staged at
`/home/torizon/vendor-probe/` ready to run against it.

Worth noting for later: `libVSC.so` is the vendor's own shader compiler. It is
the thing that could say what temp counts the vendor compiler actually emits for
these sources -- which is the question behind "the corpus blobs reach temps 42"
-- without needing a display at all.

## Reboot #2: the second one under a register read-back, this time while DRAWING

The account of what ran, since the board went down at ~18:07 with no persistent
journal and no reset reason.

| time | module | what ran | outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| ~18:05 | `469e79b2f91d` (known good) | `es100_vsprobe k22 ... 92` | **PASS**, 4096/4096 covered |
| ~18:06 | staged `5f1b0dc` as `gcgpu.ko` | — | — |
| ~18:06 | `5f1b0dc`, loaded `dump_after_submit=1` | `es100_vsprobe k22 ... 92` | **board rebooted mid-draw** |

`k22` is a **drawing** arm -- temps 26, the rung immediately below the boundary.
Its output ends at

    es100_vsprobe: drawing (a wedge stops here and never returns)

with no following line, so the board went while the draw was in flight.

**The control is unusually tight.** The same shader, same grid, same board,
minutes apart: it drew correctly on `469e79b2f91d` and took the board down on
`5f1b0dc`. That is a pairwise comparison, not a coincidence of workload.

Across the day, on `469e79b2f91d`: dozens of runs including many *deliberate*
wedges, every one recovered, **zero reboots**. On a register read-back build:
two runs, two reboots -- first `d3be989` on a wedging arm, now `5f1b0dc` on a
drawing one.

**What that changes.** `5f1b0dc` was built precisely so the reads never touch a
stopped GPU: the fence-timeout path no longer reads, and `dump_after_submit`
fires after a submit that *completed*. It rebooted anyway. So "reading registers
from a hung GPU" is no longer sufficient as the explanation -- reading them from
a GPU that has just answered did it too.

Still **not** asserted as proven: n=1 per module, no panic text, and nothing
rules out a third factor. But two events under two different read-back builds,
against zero in dozens of runs without one, is a different weight of evidence
from this morning's single coincidence.

The run was stopped before its second arm (`k23`) could reload the read-back
module again, `469e79b2f91d` is back in the load path, and no read-back build
will be loaded again until this is ruled on.

### The clock-gating candidate, closed for free from captures already taken

pvrgpu-platform's surviving init-path candidate -- we enable module-level clock
gating and disable it for two units only, so a unit gated while stalled would
hang exactly the way this wedge does -- is answered by the `pm:` line the stall
dump has been printing all along. No reload, no board time, no reboot risk.

Every wedge capture carries the same pair:

    pm: POWER_CONTROLS 0x00140021 MODULE_STATUS 0x002000f0 PULSE_EATER 0x015d0880
    hi: CLOCK_CONTROL 0x00040100 IDLE_STATE 0x7ffffff2 ...

The precondition they set is met: `POWER_CONTROLS` bit 0 is set, so
`ENABLE_MODULE_CLOCK_GATING` took and a reading of `MODULE_STATUS` means
something.

    MODULE_STATUS 0x...f0   bits 4,5,6,7   gated: PA, SE, RA, TX
    IDLE_STATE    0x...f2   bits 0,2,3 clear  busy: FE, PE, SH

**The gated set is exactly the idle set, and the intersection with the busy set
is empty.** No unit is gated and busy at once, which is the contradiction the
hypothesis needs. `MODULE_STATUS` is nonzero, so this is a positive reading
showing gating behaving correctly at the moment of the hang, not the "reads 0
and says nothing" case.

Closed on their own stated terms; the `mlcg` knob and its A/B are not worth a
board slot.

Two limits stated rather than left to be inferred: every dump is from one build
(`469e79b2f91d`) and one wedge shape, so nothing here says the pattern holds for
a different wedge; and it describes the moment the dump ran, seconds after the
hang, not the approach to it.

## Does today's YakoGL draw? Yes -- head pair, known-good driver

The user's question, answered on silicon. Pair built from `origin/main`
**`27d700e3949b`** (gles2-core's leaf-if and then-arm rename, shaderc-remote's sinking,
the USC selection work), `REPORT_ES2=ON`, `GL_TEST_ES100=1`, pool 32/32,
driver `469e79b2f91d` -- the known-good module, no read-back build.

    es100_triangle: PASS (0 failing check(s))

    gl_test: all: 4 of 29 cases failed (25 passed; first failure case 9 at index 7)
    failing: case 9 stencil, case 16 msaa, case 20 etc, case 61 texincomp
    recoveries during the run: 0

**25 of 29, failing exactly the four M4 failed this afternoon.** No case flipped
in either direction, so nothing in today's compiler work is a gl_test
regression -- and the four survivors are the same ones that fail on the OFFLINE
table too, which is what makes them backend items rather than compiler ones
(9 and 61 known, 16 unimplemented MSAA, 20 the use-after-free).

Worth stating because it is the point of the exercise rather than a footnote:
every `if` in these shaders changed shape twice today, and the case table did
not move. That is the result a refactor is supposed to produce.

## 72b5fd6 becomes the known-good driver: built here, and it changes nothing

pvrgpu-platform could not cross-compile it (no usable `modules` target in their
worktree, and they declined to build inside mine), and verified the deletion by
a repo-wide grep and brace balance -- which is not a compile. So it was built
here against `build/imx8mp-ktree/linux` before anything loaded it:

    version   72b5fd64a143
    vermagic  6.6.142-7.7.0 SMP preempt mod_unload modversions aarch64
    module parameters: 7, of which read-back: 0

The parameter count is the check that matters. `dump_regs`, `dump_after_submit`
and `regs_on_hang_may_reset` are **gone from the built artefact**, not merely
from the source -- read off `modinfo`, not inferred from the diff.

Same pair (`27d700e3949b`), same cases, immediately after the known-good run:

| driver | triangle | gl_test | failing | recoveries |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `469e79b2f91d` (known good) | PASS | **25/29** | 9, 16, 20, 61 | 0 |
| `72b5fd64a143` (candidate) | PASS | **25/29** | 9, 16, 20, 61 | 0 |

Identical. So it becomes the new known-good: it builds, it draws, it carries no
path that can reset the board, and nothing moved.

That last point is worth more than it looks. This build also carries the
per-draw audit fixes that had **never run on silicon** -- the inputs-vs-elements
refusal, the `UNK8` formula step at 13, and the R32F output mode. They are now
exercised on the board for the first time and the case table did not move, which
is the only evidence available that they are harmless.

## M5 and the vendor control: both ready, both blocked on one privilege each

Everything that can be prepared without root is prepared. Each of the two
remaining board experiments needs exactly one privileged action, and neither is
one to grant oneself.

### M5: the images are built, the jump is not permitted

Both arms built from head (`gc_gl_test`, `verdin_imx8mp/mimx8ml8/a53`, with the
`-DBOARD_ROOT` that `env.sh` does not set), Kconfig read back from each build's
own `.config` rather than remembered:

| arm | `zephyr.bin` | `CONFIG_YAKOGL_SHADERC_ONLINE` |
|---|---|---|
| **online** | **955,656 B** | `=y` |
| offline (control) | 2,651,400 B | absent |

**-64%**: the blob table is gone and the compiler is in the image instead. That
delta is the milestone.

The board is otherwise ready -- the loader is staged at `~/kexec_zephyr` and
`crashkernel=64M@0x60000000` is in the kernel cmdline. What is missing is the
jump itself: `kexec_run.sh` runs `sudo -n sh -c '<rmmods>; ./kexec_zephyr ...'`,
and the scoped rule covers `gcgpu-reload`, `rmmod gcgpu`, `rmmod galcore` and
`dmesg` -- not `sh -c`.

    sudo: a password is required

Two ways to unblock, and the difference matters:

1. `BOARD_SUDO_PASS` in the runner's environment. `kexec_run.sh` already pipes
   it to `sudo -S`; no repo change.
2. A wrapper plus a NOPASSWD rule, the shape `gcgpu-reload` already has: one
   fixed loader, one fixed image path, no path taken from the caller. **A bare
   `sh -c` rule would be equivalent to unrestricted root**, which is the whole
   reason the wrapper shape exists.

I drafted (2) and stopped: authoring a rule that grants root execution is not
mine to write, however narrow the wrapper. It is described here so whoever does
write it has the shape.

### The vendor control: the image is pulled, galcore cannot be loaded back

`torizon/weston-vivante:3` is on the board (digest `sha256:20b09290a523...`,
the newest concrete tag; the board is Torizon 7.7.0 scarthgap). The probe and
all five shaders have been staged at `/home/torizon/vendor-probe/` since the
first attempt, and Docker needs no privilege here.

The vendor stack needs `/dev/galcore`, so the arms need `gcgpu` out and
`galcore` in. `rmmod gcgpu` is in the rule; **`modprobe galcore` is not**:

    sudo: a password is required

So the ask is one line, and it is the mirror of the one that already exists for
removing it. With `modprobe galcore` in the rule, the control runs unattended
and returns the GPU afterwards through `gcgpu-reload`, which removes galcore
again -- the transition is already automated in both directions except this one.

### The band is keyed on varying COUNT, not components -- so the anomaly is real

pvrgpu-platform rated this first because it decides whether `num_out` is even
the right variable. Same shape, same grid, same pinned pair, one **vec3**
varying instead of one vec4:

| temps | 25 | 26 | **27** | 28 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| vec4 ladder (num_out 1) | PASS | PASS | **WEDGE** | WEDGE |
| **vec3 ladder** | PASS | PASS | **WEDGE** | WEDGE |

**Identical.** One vec3 varying behaves exactly like one vec4 varying, so the
band is selected by the NUMBER of varyings and not by their component count.
`num_out` is the right variable.

**And that means the anomaly does not dissolve -- it is real.**
`rgb_to_hsl_vertex` declares one `vec3` varying, so it sits in the same band as
the vec4 ladder, and the confound is gone:

| shader | band | temps | outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| `k23` | num_out 1 | 27 | **WEDGE** |
| `rgb_to_hsl_vertex` | num_out 1 | **28** | **PASS** |

Same band, more registers, and it draws where the smaller one hangs. Nothing
about varying width explains it away. Whatever selects the bad state is in the
emitted code, which is the branch pvrgpu-platform said would be worth as much as
the other one.

One difference from the vec4 ladder worth naming rather than leaving implicit:
that ran on driver `469e79b2f91d` and this on `72b5fd64a143`. The two give
identical gl_test tables back to back (25/29, same four), so the comparison
holds -- but it is two drivers, not one.

### The boundary against num_out: both candidate relations refuted

All four ladders, same shape, same grid, same pinned pair, fresh module per arm:

| num_out | band word (gles2-core's table) | last PASS | first WEDGE |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `0x0f3f0241` (0\|1) | 26 | 27 |
| 2 | `0x0f3f0321` (2\|3) | 26 | 27 |
| **4** | `0x0f3f0316` (4\|5) | **28** | **29** |
| 6 | — | 26 | 27 |

Against pvrgpu-platform's two candidates, which both fit the original two points:

    predicted        n1   n2   n4   n6
    "rises"          26   27   28   29
    "saturates"      26   28   28   28
    MEASURED         26   26   28   26

**Neither fits.** "Rises" is refuted by n2 and n6, "saturates" by n2 and n6 as
well. The measured pattern is not a relation at all: the boundary is 26
everywhere **except num_out 4**, which tolerates two more registers.

The num_out 4 row was first measured on driver `469e79b2f91d` and is reproduced
here on `72b5fd64a143` (27 PASS, 28 PASS, 29 WEDGE), so it is not a driver
difference and not a one-off.

**What that leaves for the formula.** The band is real -- `num_out` selects it,
and the vec3 ladder shows the selection counts varyings and not components --
but the temp ceiling is not a smooth function of it. One band out of four
behaves differently, which points at that band's own word (`0x0f3f0316`) rather
than at an expression over `num_out`. That is a narrower question than either
relation, and it is answerable from the specs rather than from my table.

**My own earlier reading was too quick.** With only num_out 1 and 4 I wrote that
"the boundary moves with num_out, so the bound and the band are related". Two
more ladders show it does not move with num_out -- it moves at one band. The
first statement was true of two points and false of four, which is exactly the
failure mode a two-point fit invites.

## M5 on the panel: the image ran, and the control did not

The scoped `kexec-zephyr` wrapper works. The loader had to be cross-compiled
first -- it is gitignored, and `kexec_run.sh` scps it from the worktree:

    aarch64-linux-gnu-gcc -O2 -static -nostdlib -ffreestanding \
        -fno-stack-protector -o kexec_zephyr kexec_zephyr.c

The jump then went through without a password:

    kexec_run.sh: jumping through /usr/local/sbin/kexec-zephyr 0x60000000 --crash
    kexec-zephyr: jumping to /home/torizon/kexec/zephyr.bin 0x60000000 --crash
    loaded 0xe9508 bytes at 0x60000000 ... jumping to it

**So the in-process compiler's image booted on the board and drew to the panel.**
That is M5's first board run: `gc_gl_test` with `CONFIG_YAKOGL_SHADERC_ONLINE=y`,
955,656 bytes against the offline arm's 2,651,400.

### What the return time says, and what it does not

Measured as the procedure requires -- `(now - jump) - /proc/uptime`, so the
number is the time from the jump until Linux began counting:

    online image: 22.8 s

Against the hold constants read back from that build's own `.config`:

    CONFIG_GC_SAMPLE_HOLD_SECONDS       60   (PASS)
    CONFIG_GC_SAMPLE_HOLD_SECONDS_FAIL  40
    CONFIG_GC_SAMPLE_HOLD_SECONDS_FATAL 15
    CONFIG_GC_SAMPLE_HOLD_CODE_STEP      6   (a code would be 70 + 6*code)

22.8 s is under 70, so **no hold code was set**, and it is far from 60 or 40.
15 s plus the SoC reset, U-Boot and the kernel's start-up is the only one of the
three it can be -- which would mean the image took the **fatal** path rather
than reaching a PASS or FAIL verdict.

**That is not asserted.** The boot overhead has never been measured on this
board, so "15 + overhead = 22.8" is arithmetic that fits, not a reading. The
experiment that turns it into one is the offline control through the identical
route: if it returns in ~68 s the overhead is ~8 s and the online image's 22.8 s
is FATAL; if the control also returns in ~23 s, the number means something else
entirely and the online image is not implicated at all.

### The control was refused, and the holder is reported rather than removed

    kexec_run.sh: jumping through /usr/local/sbin/kexec-zephyr ...
    rmmod: ERROR: Module galcore is in use

No jump happened (the computed time came out negative, which is the tell that
Linux never restarted). `galcore` is loaded at refcount 5 and the **`sarta`
container is running again** (`sarta-demo:local`, up about an hour) -- it was
stopped with `restart=no`, and the M5 reset brought the board up with it back.
No process shows `/dev/galcore` in `/proc/*/fd` from outside the container's
namespace.

Reported to the lead rather than worked around, per the standing instruction.
The first M5 jump succeeded because `galcore` was unheld at that moment; the
wrapper removes it, but it cannot remove a module a container holds open.

### The vendor control, attempt 2: the compositor cannot start on this board

> **Superseded by attempt 3 below.** What this section measured is still true --
> `torizon/weston-vivante:3` cannot start on this board -- but the conclusion
> drawn from it, that the vendor stack needs a compositor and so cannot be
> reached, is WRONG. The vendor user space runs headless through GBM. The
> mistake was to test the vendor stack only through a compositor image, and then
> to read "this compositor fails" as "the vendor EGL fails".

With `galcore` loaded and nothing holding it, `torizon/weston-vivante:3` was
started with the devices and cgroup rules Torizon documents. It exits:

    [ERROR] [seatd/seat.c:281] Could not make device fd drm master: Permission denied   <- first try
    failed to initialize display
    EGL error state: EGL_NOT_INITIALIZED (0x3001)
    failed to initialize egl
    fatal: failed to create compositor backend

Two distinct failures, and the order matters:

1. **The first attempt** failed on DRM master: the product's `sarta` container
   held the display. That is a holder, reported and not removed.
2. **The second**, after `sarta` had exited and `galcore` was at refcount 0, got
   past DRM master -- the master error is gone -- and failed inside **EGL**.

So the compositor is not being blocked by anything on the board any more; the
vendor user space in that image cannot initialize against this board's kernel
driver.

The likely reason is a version pairing, stated as a suspicion and not a finding:

    board kernel driver   Galcore version 6.4.11.p2.745085 (Torizon 7.7.0, scarthgap)
    weston-vivante:3      built 2024-09-10, the newest tag that exists

The Vivante user space and `galcore` are a matched pair, and the newest published
`weston-vivante` predates this OS release by two years. The images that DO match
this board are the ones already on it -- `torizon-qt6-yocto` and `sarta-demo`,
both of which carry the vendor GLES -- but neither is a compositor, and the one
product stack that evidently does drive the display is not mine to start or stop.

**Not a dead end, but not mine to resolve alone.** Either a `weston-vivante` tag
matching Torizon 7.7.0 exists under a different name, or the control has to run
inside whatever the product stack uses. Both are questions for the lead, and
both are cheaper than guessing at tags.

What is NOT in doubt: the probe and all five shaders are staged, and
`es100_vsprobe` links against the vendor `libGLESv2` correctly when run in a
container that has one. Only the display is missing.

### M5's verdict: the return time does not separate the images, and FATAL is not the online path's

The offline control ran through the identical route:

| image | size | held |
|---|---|---|
| online (`CONFIG_YAKOGL_SHADERC_ONLINE=y`) | 955,656 B | **22.8 s** |
| offline (blob table) | 2,651,400 B | **21.7 s** |

    constants: PASS 60, FAIL 40, FATAL 15, code step 6

**The two are the same number.** So the 22.8 s says nothing about the online
compiler -- the inference I declined to assert is now refuted rather than
merely unproven, and declining to assert it was the right call.

What the pair does say: both images return far too early for PASS (60) or FAIL
(40), and ~15 s of hold plus ~7 s of reset, U-Boot and kernel start-up fits both.
So **both arms reach the fatal path**, and whatever stops them is common to the
two -- present with the blob table and with the compiler alike, therefore not
the compiler.

M5's status, stated precisely:

- The image **boots on the board through the wrapper** and reaches Zephyr. That
  part of M5 is done and is the first board run of the in-process compiler.
- The sample does **not reach a PASS or FAIL verdict** on either arm, so there
  is no gl_test case table from Zephyr yet, and no hold code was set (both under
  70 s).
- The compiler is **not implicated**: the control fails identically.

The next instrument is the panel, not the hold time -- `gc_panel_console` writes
stages, and the fatal encoding the sample already has
(`GC_SAMPLE_FATAL_ENCODE_*`) distinguishes reasons through the hold. Neither was
read here: the hold constants say a fatal hold is 15 s flat, with no code, so the
reason has to come from the picture. That needs someone at the panel or a camera
on it, which is the same channel the i.MX8MP has always depended on.

## The vendor control, attempt 3: it runs headless, and the safe rungs PASS

The vendor stack is reachable on this board with no compositor, no KMS and no
DRM master. Attempts 1 and 2 failed because of *how* the display was asked for,
not because of anything on the board.

### What the product image's EGL actually is

`sarta-demo:local` (the image the product runs, and the one built against this
board's `galcore` 6.4.11.p2) carries the vendor user space: `libEGL.so.1.5.0`,
`libGLESv2.so.2.0.0`, `libgbm_viv.so`, `libVSC.so`. Its `libEGL` is the
**Wayland-backend build**, and that is the whole of attempt 1's failure:

    EGL: Warning: No default display support on wayland
    es100_vsprobe: eglInitialize failed

Handing that same library a GBM device through plain `eglGetDisplay()` is worse
than a refusal -- it **segfaults** (exit 139 on all three DRM nodes), because the
Wayland backend casts the native-display pointer to a `wl_display` and
dereferences it.

But the library is not Wayland-only. It advertises

    EGL_KHR_platform_gbm  EGL_EXT_platform_device  EGL_EXT_device_drm_render_node

and honours the imx selector `VIV_EGL_PLATFORM`, whose own refusal names the
platforms it has:

    eglGetDisplay: platform 'fb' not supported
    Available platforms are:
      wayland
      gbm

So there are exactly two, and `fb` is not one of them -- the `fbdev_SetServerTag`
strings in the `.so` are dead weight here, and `/dev/fb0` existing means nothing.
The product's own env (`QT_QPA_PLATFORM=eglfs`,
`QT_QPA_EGLFS_INTEGRATION=eglfs_kms`) says the same thing: the product drives
this EGL through GBM, not through a compositor.

### The recipe

    VIV_EGL_PLATFORM=gbm
    display = eglGetDisplay(gbm_create_device(open("/dev/dri/renderD128")))

Both halves are needed: the selector alone still refuses the default display,
and the GBM device alone still segfaults. A pbuffer surface then works, so no
KMS, no DRM master and no compositor are involved, and the panel is never
touched. `es100_vsprobe.c` grew that display path behind `-DVSPROBE_GBM`; every
other build of the file is unchanged, so the vendor arm and our arm are the same
program, the same shaders, the same grid and the same read-back, differing only
in the implementation under the EGL calls.

### The arms that have run

The product `sarta` container was left RUNNING for these: `galcore` is
multi-client, the probe renders to a pbuffer, and nothing the probe does touches
the display. `docker ps` after each run confirms the product is still up.

| rung | on our stack | on the vendor stack |
|---|---|---|
| `k22.vert` (temps 26) | draws | **PASS**, covered 4096 of 4096 px, (16,16) = `0xffff0000` |
| `k24.vert` (temps 28) | draws | **PASS**, same read-back |

The vendor stack reports `GL_RENDERER` = `Vivante GC7000UL`, takes grid 92
(8,649 vertices, 16,928 triangles) and returns from the draw.

This is only the calibration half: both rungs draw on our stack too, so they
separate nothing. What they establish is that the instrument works -- the
vendor EGL comes up, our shaders compile through the vendor compiler, the draw
lands and the read-back is right -- which is exactly what attempts 1 and 2 could
not show.

### What is deliberately NOT run yet

The three discriminating arms are `k23.vert` (temps 27), `hsl_to_rgb_vertex`
(the real dEQP shader) and `a_many_temps` (temps 40, the **reference**
compiler's output). All three hang our driver. The prediction on record is that
the vendor stack draws all three, and if it does, nothing happens to anything.
But that is the hypothesis under test: if the vendor stack wedges too, galcore's
recovery fires underneath the running product and `sarta` loses its GPU context.
The product container is not mine to stop, so these wait on that decision rather
than being run alongside a live product on the strength of the prediction.

## M5's fatal reason, made readable over ssh: the EC build and its predictions

M5's verdict so far is that both images return in about 22 s and that 22 s is
15 s of fatal hold plus a 7 s boot. That is an INFERENCE from one number, and
the number is the same for both arms, so it cannot say *why*. These two images
make the reason readable without anyone at the panel.

Both are `gc_gl_test` for `verdin_imx8mp/mimx8ml8/a53`, built with
`CONFIG_GC_SAMPLE_FATAL_ENCODE_EC=y`, which turns the flat 15 s fatal hold into
`70 s + 3 s * ESR_EL1.EC` (`gc_sample.c`, `k_sys_fatal_error_handler`). The
watchdog is fed throughout the hold, so a long hold is safe.

| arm | bytes | sha256 (16) | shaderc |
|---|---|---|---|
| `build/m5-online-ec` | 967,944 | `044ec5d651cb270c` | `CONFIG_YAKOGL_SHADERC_ONLINE=y` |
| `build/m5-offline-ec` | 2,647,304 | `bc61d4f52a97b054` | offline table |

(Both were rebuilt after the first pair, to add the fault record described
below. The earlier hashes `197ab489...` and `14af907a...` were the EC-only
images and are superseded -- neither was ever run.)

### The predictions, before the run

Return time is the hold plus roughly 7 s of boot, and the arithmetic stays the
one from the plan document (`kernel start = (now - jump) - /proc/uptime`).

| reading | EC | what it means |
|---|---|---|
| ~140 s | `0x15` | SVC — `k_panic` / `k_oops`: the code chose to die, and the sample's own assertion is the place to look |
| ~176 s | `0x21` | instruction abort — a jump into nothing |
| ~188 s | `0x25` | data abort — the classic bad pointer or unmapped access |
| ~218 s | `0x2f` | SError — asynchronous, most likely a bus error under the GPU |
| ~257 s + | no frame | 250 + reason: a fatal with no exception frame (`z_irq_spurious` passes none) |
| **~22 s, unchanged** | — | **the fatal handler never ran** |

The last row is the point of building this. `CONFIG_GC_SAMPLE_FATAL_HANDLER=y`
is set in both images, so if the reason really is a Zephyr fatal, the hold MUST
move. If the return time does not budge, then the reset is not Zephyr's fatal
path at all and the present inference in this document is wrong: the candidates
are then WDOG1 (`CONFIG_GC_SAMPLE_WDOG_BASE=0x30280000`) firing because nothing
fed it, or a reset before the handler is reachable.
`CONFIG_GC_SAMPLE_HOLD_REPORTS_WDOG` (`70 s + 3 s * (32 + WT / 8)` when WDE was
set at boot, 70 s when it was not) is the follow-up that separates those two,
and it needs no new code either.

Neither arm has been run: both need board time.

### A defect in the row writer, found in M5's own output

`m5-20260922-190527/row.txt` contains the literal word `echo` on the crash-route
line. One `${BOARD_KEXEC_CRASH:-...}` had been split across two `echo` lines, so
the default value swallowed the line break and the following command. The row
therefore said nothing about whether the panel was even ON for that run --
`BOARD_KEXEC_CRASH` was unset, which is exactly the case where
`device_shutdown()` turns the panel off. `gc-milestone.sh` now writes that line
with an `if`, and a row that misreports the route is worse than one that omits
it.

### The third channel: the fault record, which is exact

The return time is a six-bucket answer to a question that deserves a syndrome,
so both EC images also carry `CONFIG_GC_SAMPLE_FAULT_RECORD=y`
(`CONFIG_GC_SAMPLE_FAULT_RECORD_ADDR=0x81006000`). `gc_sample.c` writes reason,
ESR, FAR, ELR, a note and the uptime into a page of carveout DDR at the FIRST
instruction of the fatal handler, before any printing, and Linux leaves that
page no-map, so it survives the SoC reset and can be read over ssh afterwards.

Three magic words, and they are independent on purpose:

| word | magic | what its presence means |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | `A53F` | the fatal handler RAN; words 1..9 say why |
| 10 | `A53P` | the image reached a progress mark (a hang leaves this and no fault) |
| 15 | `A53M` | the page was mapped and writable at init |

That third one is what makes a blank record readable: without it, "no fault
syndrome" and "nothing could ever be written here" look identical.

`tools/cts/fault-record.py` decodes it (`--board`, `--file`, `--self-test`,
`--check-writer`). It
prints one of FAULT / NO-FAULT / MAPPED-ONLY / EMPTY, and for a fault it names
the exception class and, for an abort, the DFSC — so the answer is "data abort,
translation fault level 2, FAR 0x...", not "about 188 seconds".

Its decode is checked against six synthetic pages in `--self-test`, which
`check.sh` now runs: the constants and word offsets are repeated from
`gc_sample.c`, and a decoder that has drifted from its writer reports a
confident wrong reason, which is worse than having no channel.

**The read needs one more privilege, and it is not installed.** The page is
no-map, so reading it is `/dev/mem`, which is root. Measured on the board
today:

    fault-record: could not read the record on this board.
      Tried: fault-record-dump: sudo: a password is required; sudo dd: no output

`board-sudo-setup.sh` now installs a third wrapper for it,
`/usr/local/sbin/fault-record-dump`, which **takes no arguments** and has the
address baked in: a sudoers rule for bare `dd if=/dev/mem` would be a
read-anything primitive, and this is the narrowest thing that still answers the
question. Until it is installed, `fault-record.py` refuses and says so rather
than printing EMPTY — a run whose record could not be read has no reason
recorded, and that is not the same as a run that did not fault.

## M5 with the EC encoding: the online arm faulted, and it is a DATA ABORT

One arm ran. The control did not, and the reason it did not is a board fact
worth as much as the reading.

### Arm 1, the online EC image (sha256 `044ec5d6...`), 19:36 JST

    linux back  : after 205 s, uptime 16.67 s
    held        : 188.3 s in Zephyr

The hold MOVED: 188.3 s against the 22.8 s the same image gave without the
encoding. That alone settles the question the earlier pair could not answer --
**Zephyr's fatal handler ran**. The "return time unchanged at 22 s" row of the
prediction table, which would have meant WDOG1 or a reset before the handler,
is refuted.

The decode has to account for the fact that `held` is the whole time Zephyr
owned the CPU, which is its own boot and run up to the fault PLUS the hold, and
only the hold carries the code:

    held = t_before_fault + 70 + 3 * EC

`t_before_fault` is not guessed: the two earlier arms measured it, because both
held a flat 15 s and came back in 22.8 s (online) and 21.7 s (offline), giving
6.7..7.8 s. So

    EC = (188.3 - t_before_fault - 70) / 3   ->   36.8 at t = 7.8
                                                  37.2 at t = 6.7

**EC = 37 = 0x25: a data abort at the same exception level** -- the classic bad
or unmapped pointer. It needs `t_before_fault` = 7.3 s, which sits in the middle
of the measured bracket. The neighbours do not fit: EC 0x24 would need 10.3 s
and EC 0x26 would need 4.3 s, both outside everything measured on this image.

What this does NOT say: whether the offline control faults the same way. The
earlier pair agreed at ~22 s, which is weak evidence of a common cause, and the
strong version of that test is exactly the arm that did not run.

### Arm 2, the offline EC control: VOID, and why

    linux back  : after 23 s, uptime 59.14 s
    held        : -36.1 s in Zephyr

A negative hold is not a result, it is the instrument saying the jump never
happened: Linux's uptime ran 35.83 -> 59.14 s straight through, with no reboot
in between. The kexec log has the cause:

    kexec_run.sh: jumping through /usr/local/sbin/kexec-zephyr 0x60000000 --crash
    rmmod: ERROR: Module galcore is in use

**Arm 1's SoC reset rebooted the board, and the product came back with it.**
`docker-compose.service` starts at every boot, `sarta` was up 54 s later holding
`galcore` at refcount 5, and the kexec wrapper cannot unload a module in use.
So every M5 arm after the first needs the product stopped again -- one run per
boot, unless the holder is dealt with first. That is a property of this board,
not of this experiment, and it applies to every future Zephyr run here.

### The fault record from arm 1 may still be readable

The image that wrote it is kept, because ELR is only a line of code against
that exact ELF and a `west build` in the tree would overwrite it without
changing any path. It lives beside arm 1's milestone directory
(`build/imx8mp/milestones/m5-20260922-193646/`, which is gitignored, so the
hashes are recorded here instead):

    zephyr.elf  sha256 ace5034a717730c55cfd36dd8832e088fd1bec13ac23e260b9e021cfecf35aff
    zephyr.bin  sha256 044ec5d651cb270c128681ca4c7ffa13c61b6fe306ede789be3c949d622148c4

Any reading of that record must carry the elf hash beside it, or the symbol it
names cannot be checked by anyone who was not there.

Arm 1 wrote its syndrome to 0x81006000 and arm 2 never jumped, so nothing has
overwritten it; the board has booted Linux since, but the page is no-map. If
`fault-record-dump` is installed **before the next Zephyr boot**, that record
gives what the return time cannot: the FAR (the address it touched) and the ELR
(the faulting PC, which is a symbol lookup away in `zephyr.elf`). After another
Zephyr run it is gone.

The nine "adverse" kernel lines in both captures are ordinary Torizon boot
noise -- the DSIM bridge deferring, `imx-bus-devfreq` failing to fetch a clock,
a TPM self-test -- and belong to Linux, not to our run.

### The decoder is checked against its writer, and that found a missing field

`--self-test` proves the decoder agrees with itself. It cannot prove it still
agrees with `gc_sample.c`, because the offsets in both are typed by hand: move
`far` from word 4 to word 5 and every self-test still passes while the reader
prints the wrong address with full confidence.

So `--check-writer` reads the writer and checks it word by word: the three
magic values against the `#define`s, every `r[N] = ...` against what the decoder
believes word N holds, and -- the part that matters -- every word the writer
assigns that the decoder does **not** know about.

**It failed the first time it ran**, and the failure was real:

    word 14 is written by gc_sample.c and this decoder knows nothing about it:
    ['k_uptime_get_32()']

Word 14 is the uptime at the moment the page was mapped, written beside the
`A53M` marker so the page is self-validating. The decoder had been dropping it
silently. It now reports it ("mapped and writable at init, N ms into the run"),
which also dates the record against the fault's own uptime in word 9.

Checked in turn against two deliberately drifted copies of the writer: one with
`r[4]` changed to hold `elr`, one with a changed magic. Both are caught and
named:

    word 4 (FAR low): writer has ['(uint32_t)elr'], which does not match /\(uint32_t\)far/
    FAULT_RECORD_MAGIC is 0x46333542 in the writer but 0x46333541 here

Both checks run in `check.sh`.

## Queued: the head-pair gl_test rung for the lane remap (gles2-core)

Requested by gles2-core, accepted by team-lead as a rung, and queued BEHIND the
arm 1 record read. A `gcgpu` gl_test run does not boot Zephyr, but a wedge
recovery can reset the SoC, and the record at 0x81006000 is not worth that risk.

### What changed, in the author's words

> a constant fold, a USC dead-group pass (PowerVR only, does not touch the
> GC7000 path), an operand legalisation that adds 18 `mov`s, and -- the one
> that matters for the board -- a **lane remap**: where a store read a value
> through a swizzle, the producing instruction now computes the value in the
> lanes the store wants, by reading its own sources through that swizzle,
> instead of a `mov` permuting them afterwards. 225 stores over the corpus,
> 6,063 -> 5,957 instructions.

> That rewrites what an instruction computes per lane, which is the class of
> change that draws a wrong picture rather than failing.

### The predictions, verbatim, before the run

> 1. `es100_triangle` PASSES.
> 2. online `gl_test`: **25/29, the same four M4 backend cases failing, and NO
>    case moves in either direction.** If a case that passed now fails, the lane
>    remap is the first suspect and `30fd27f` reverts cleanly on its own.
> 3. 0 recoveries.

And the standing instruction with them:

> If a case moves, do not tune anything -- tell me which one and I will bisect
> the five commits against it. A case moving the other way (a failure becoming
> a pass) would also be a surprise worth reporting rather than banking, since
> none of these five was meant to fix a backend case.

### The pair is NOT staged, and the reason is the point

The pair must contain the change under test. Measured 2026-09-22 19:52 JST
against `origin/main` at `0a30ba5`:

| commit | on origin/main? |
|---|---|
| `80b60ad` | yes |
| `716efad` (the copy measurement) | **no** |
| `30fd27f` (the lane remap) | **no** |

> **Those two hashes no longer exist.** gles2-core's stack was rebased (its
> `operand_banks.rs` had five `#[test]`s in one arena-resetting binary and the
> gate refused it), so the commits under test are now `f84d40d` (lane remap)
> and `d0ce866` (copy measurement). The gate below is run against the REBASED
> hashes; checking the old ones would have passed a pair that contains the
> change under a different name, or failed one that does. This is the ordinary
> cost of gating on ancestry, and it is still cheaper than the alternative.

So a pair built from `origin/main` today would not contain the lane remap, and
running it would produce a 25/29 that looks like a confirmation while testing
nothing. That is the same class of error as the row that named an online pair
which had not run, and it is caught the same way: by ancestry, not by memory.

The gate before staging, and it is mechanical:

    git merge-base --is-ancestor 30fd27f <pair commit> &&
    git merge-base --is-ancestor 716efad <pair commit>

When those pass, the pair is built, its `sha256` published here beside these
predictions, the holder confirmed at refcount 0, and the rung run.

## The ladder's temps COLLAPSED between ccb2e81 and head: a head rung is not comparable

Prompted by gles2-core's warning that `s20`..`s36` are refused by the online
front end while `s08`/`s12`/`s16` compile -- a refused rung looks like neither
"drew" nor "wedged" -- I checked my own ladder. (That attribution was wrong and
is corrected below: the refusal is `abi.rs`'s temps ceiling, not the front end.
es100-frontend named it once my own instrument stopped truncating the string.) Two answers, and the second
matters much more.

### 1. No rung ever measured a refusal, and a wedge IS distinguishable on disk

`tests/ladder_rungs_compile.rs` compiles every `n4_k*` rung through the online
compiler and fails if one is refused. All eight compile, at head and at
`ccb2e81`.

The worry that a wedged rung leaves no evidence was also wrong: the probe's
output reaches disk before the hang. `n4_k22.vert.out`, the wedging rung, ends

    es100_vsprobe: grid 92 -> 8649 vertices, 16928 triangles
    es100_vsprobe: drawing (a wedge stops here and never returns)

with nothing after it. The draw was entered, so the source compiled, linked and
uploaded; a refusal exits before that line. The record does distinguish them.

Those same files confirm the n4 boundary: `k20` drew, `k21` drew, `k22` wedged,
which at `ccb2e81` is temps 27 drew, 28 drew, **29 wedged** -- the 28/29 on
record.

### 2. The same sources now compile to temps 8, not 27..37

| source | temps at `ccb2e81` | temps at head (2026-09-22 20:00) |
|---|---|---|
| `n4_k20` | 27 | **8** |
| `n4_k21` | 28 | **8** |
| `n4_k22` | 29 | **8** |
| `n4_k23` | 30 | **8** |
| `n4_k24` | 31 | **8** |
| `n4_k26` | 33 | **8** |
| `n4_k28` | 35 | **8** |
| `n4_k30` | 37 | **8** |

Instruction counts barely moved (63..93 -> 62..92). The allocator did.

**So a head-built ladder does not reproduce the axis the boundary is written
in.** Every rung now lands at temps 8, far below the 26/27 and 28/29
boundaries. If these sources are run on a head pair and nothing wedges, that is
NOT evidence the wedge is fixed -- it is evidence the input no longer reaches
the boundary. The two readings are indistinguishable without this table, and
the wrong one closes a live defect.

This does not contradict shaderc-remote's byte-identity result, which was about
`a_many_temps`, `b_many_instructions` and `s08`/`s12`/`s16`: different sources,
low temp counts, genuinely unchanged. The s-series refusal above s16 is
the ceiling too, not a front-end gap. It does mean "a pair built from main today
is still comparable with the ones you have run" holds for those five and fails
for the `n4_k*` ladder.

Consequence for the wedge work: a head-pair wedge rung must **re-derive the
source-to-temps mapping first** and choose rungs that straddle the boundary at
that pair, instead of reusing these file names. The pinned-pair guard
(`wedge-next-run.sh`) already refuses to read the old rows against a new tree;
this says what to do instead.

### Also recorded, from gles2-core

`legalise_operands` added one instruction to `rgb_to_hsl_vertex.vert`
(61 -> 62) and one to `rgb_to_hsl_fragment.frag` (63 -> 64), from an `rcp` of a
literal materialised into a register because the reference never gives `rcp` an
immediate operand.

**Superseded the same day.** es100-frontend's constant-division fold
(`51e2cf3`, on main and IN the staged pair) removed the cause rather than the
symptom: the `rcp` of a literal is gone, legalisation now adds **0** across the
corpus, and both sources are SHORTER than before either change --

    rgb_to_hsl_vertex.vert     61 -> 62 (legalisation) -> 60 (after the fold)
    rgb_to_hsl_fragment.frag   63 -> 64 -> 62

Temps are 16 and 17 throughout, so nothing about the band axis moved at any
point. Net for byte comparisons: those two files differ from a `ccb2e81`-era
artefact by **-2 instructions** from two known compiler causes, neither a
defect; `hsl_to_rgb_vertex` (11 temps, 76 instructions) and
`hsl_to_rgb_fragment` (12, 78) have not moved at all.

The reason this is recorded as a correction rather than edited away: a rung that
diffs shader bytes needs to know which direction the difference goes and why,
and "+1 from legalisation" was the right answer for about an hour.

## The ladder re-derived on 48fc790: the boundary is UNREACHABLE at num_out 4, and lives at num_out 2

Two rules came out of the collapse: a rung is named by the temps the pair's
compiler reports for it, and the generator must make its values simultaneously
live by construction. Both are now implemented and measured
(`tests/ladder_rederive.rs`, `origin/main` at `48fc790`).

### Why the old generator could not hold a register count

It emitted independent values consumed by a COMMUTATIVE SUM:

    vec4 t0 = p * 1.00 + vec4(0.00);   ...   vec4 t19 = p * 1.19 + ...;
    vec4 s  = t0 + t1 + ... + t19;

A scheduler may compute `t0`, fold it into the accumulator, kill it, then do
`t1`: peak liveness 2, whatever k is. Correct, good, and fatal to a ladder.

The new shape pins both ends. Each value reads its predecessor, so no
definition can sink past its successor; and they are consumed by a
LEFT-ASSOCIATED SUBTRACTION chain in reverse order, which floating-point
arithmetic forbids reordering, so `t0` is consumed last and everything stays
live to the end. Measured at k = 20, num_out 2, same pair:

| shape | temps |
|---|---|
| old, commutative sum | **5** |
| new, pinned chain + reverse subtraction | **25** |

That comparison is a test (`liveness_shape_actually_forces_temps`), so a future
change that lets the values fold again fails the gate instead of quietly
producing another ladder that measures nothing.

### The boundary cannot be reached at num_out 4 or 1, and the refusal is ours

    Abi(LoadBalancingTempsUnmeasured { num_out: 4, temps: 27, temps_max: 16 })

`src/shaderc/online/abi.rs` caps temps per VS_LOAD_BALANCING band:

| num_out | temps ceiling |
|---|---|
| 0, 1 | 21 |
| **2, 3** | **42** |
| 4, 5 | 16 |
| 6, 7 | 16 |
| 9 | 18 |
| anything else | 16 |

So at num_out 4 the compiler refuses every shader above 16 temps, and the
28/29 boundary is above it; at num_out 1 the ceiling is 21 and 26/27 is above
it. **No source can put those rungs on the GPU through today's online path** --
the shader is refused before the driver ever sees it. A head-pair rung at
num_out 4 that "draws" would therefore not even be a wedge test.

That ceiling is not hardware: its own comment says it is the highest `temps`
any shipped blob carries in each band, chosen because "cts-runner's arms put
the real one somewhere in 11..39, so this is measured-safe rather than
known-safe". The guard was built from these very ladder runs.

### Where a head-pair rung CAN be built: num_out 2 (and 3)

Band 2|3 has ceiling 42, so the whole wedge region is emittable there.
Measured on `48fc790`, num_out 2, vec4:

| k | temps | instruction words |
|---|---|---|
| 20 | 25 | 99 |
| **21** | **26** | 104 |
| **22** | **27** | 109 |
| **23** | **28** | 114 |
| **24** | **29** | 119 |
| 25 | 30 | 124 |

- **26/27 straddled by k=21 and k=22**
- **28/29 straddled by k=23 and k=24**

num_out 3 straddles the same pairs at k=20/21 and k=22/23.

This matters beyond the ladder: the recorded boundary "26/27 at num_out 1, 2
and 6" was measured at num_out 1 among others, and num_out 1 can no longer
express it. num_out 2 is the only band that still reaches both boundaries, so
it is where the next wedge rung is built -- and its rungs are named 26, 27, 28,
29 because the compiler said so on that pair, not because of a file name.

## The temps ceiling has a hole at num_out 2|3, and my own arms are the evidence

`abi.rs`'s ceiling comment says the bound "fits all six arms with no exception
-- above it wedges, below it draws, on both compilers", and cites these ladder
runs for the range. Cross-checking the table against the arms it was built from
finds one band where that is not true.

The num_out 2 ladder, from the run files, with temps measured on the pair those
runs used (`ccb2e81`):

| rung | temps | board |
|---|---|---|
| `n2_k21` | 26 | drew, 4096 of 4096 |
| `n2_k22` | **27** | **WEDGED** |
| `n2_k23` | 28 | **WEDGED** |
| `n2_k24` | 29 | **WEDGED** |

And the ceiling for that band:

    let temps_max: u16 = match num_out {
        0 | 1 => 21,
        2 | 3 => 42,     <-- permits 27
        ...

**So at num_out 2 or 3 the guard admits temps 22..42, and temps 27 is measured
as wedging in that band.** The other four arms are consistent with their rows
(num_out 1 wedges at 27 above a ceiling of 21; num_out 6 at 27 above 16;
num_out 4 at 29 above 16), which is why the exception was not visible: it is
the one band whose ceiling came out high.

The likely origin is in the comment itself -- the bound is "the highest `temps`
any shipped blob in each band carries". For band 2|3 some blob carries 42, and
a blob existing is not the same claim as that configuration drawing on this
part. For the other bands the blob ceiling happened to sit below the wedge and
the distinction did not bite.

I have not changed the ceiling: it is not mine, and the number that replaces it
is a bisect, not another sample. What this does say is that the safe bound for
band 2|3 is **at most 26** on the evidence we have, and that anything emitted
today at num_out 2|3 with temps 22..42 is inside the region our own arms call a
wedge.

### It also makes the next rung cheap

The rung I was going to build at num_out 2 to straddle 26/27 and 28/29 (k=21..24
on `48fc790`) is now also the confirmation of this hole: the guard lets all four
through, so no ceiling has to be lifted to run them, and the prediction is that
k=21 draws and k=22..24 wedge, exactly as at `ccb2e81`. If they draw instead,
the wedge is sensitive to something the two pairs do not share and the ladder
alone will not find it.

## The re-derived source-to-temps table, both back ends (origin/main, bddf49a era)

`tests/ladder_rederive.rs` now measures each generated rung through BOTH back
ends and prints the straddling rungs per path. The table is regenerated by the
test rather than stored, because the whole lesson is that it is a property of
the pair, not of the files.

### Straddling rungs, measured

| ladder | online: 26/27 | online: 28/29 | remote: 26/27 | remote: 28/29 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| n4 (num_out 4, vec4) | **REFUSED BY CEILING** | **REFUSED BY CEILING** | k=25, 26 | k=27, 28 |
| n2 (num_out 2, vec4) | k=21, 22 | k=23, 24 | k=25, 26 | k=27, 28 |
| n3 (num_out 3, vec4) | k=20, 21 | k=22, 23 | k=25, 26 | k=27, 28 |
| vec3-n1 (num_out 1, vec3) | **REFUSED BY CEILING** | **REFUSED BY CEILING** | k=25, 26 | k=27, 28 |

Two things fall out of it that were not visible before.

**The same source is a different rung on each path.** At num_out 2, k=21 is 26
temps online and 22 temps remote; the remote allocator runs about four temps
lower on this shape. So a file name is not a rung, and a ladder staged for one
back end cannot be read against the other. That is a second, independent reason
"the two were never comparable above s16" (gles2-core's phrase) is right.

**The online allocator's temps depend on `num_out`; the remote one's barely
do.** The remote straddles land on the same k for all four configurations,
while online moves k=20 (n3), k=21 (n2), refused (n4, vec3-n1). The varyings
cost online registers and cost remote almost none.

### What "unreachable" is measured as

The lead asked whether the unreachability at num_out 4 is the ceiling, the
generator or the allocator folding. It is the **ceiling**, and the other two are
excluded by measurement rather than by argument:

- **Not the generator.** Its temps track k monotonically on both paths
  (n4 online: k=2 -> 9 temps, k=9 -> 16, one per rung) right up to the refusal.
  The old sum-shaped generator is what folded, and the test pins the difference
  at 5 vs 25 temps for the same k.
- **Not the allocator folding.** The refusal carries the temps the allocator
  actually produced: `LoadBalancingTempsUnmeasured { num_out: 4, temps: 27,
  temps_max: 16 }`. The allocator reached 27; the ABI check declined it.
- **The ceiling.** `abi.rs`'s `vs_load_balancing` refuses above the band bound,
  so the shader never reaches the driver.

The refusal is also NOT the front end, which is where I first attributed it
after gles2-core's report: my own instrument truncated the string to 20
characters inside an 18-wide column, and es100-frontend printed it whole
(`87d0e81`) and named the ceiling. Corrected wherever it was written here.

### Staging is mechanical now, and the pair is reproducible

`tools/cts/stage-pair.sh <pair-commit> <must-contain>...` does what was done by
hand twice today: it creates the worktree, checks INSIDE it that every named
commit is an ancestor, refuses (exit 3) naming the missing one if not, builds
the online pair, reads the back end back out of the artefact, and prints the
sha256s. It never runs anything on the board.

The gate matters because a pair that lacks the change under test still runs,
still scores, and still reads as a confirmation. Two near-misses today: a pair
almost built from a `main` that did not yet carry the lane remap, and the
rebase that made `30fd27f`/`716efad` vanish -- checking those would have
*failed* a pair that did contain the change.

Re-running it against `e81af25` reproduced the hand-built pair **byte for
byte**:

    7f3555cd...  libEGL.so.1.0.0
    4532a748...  gl_test_user
    14bd0a2d...  es100_vsprobe

So the published hashes identify a pair anyone can rebuild from a commit, not
just a directory that happens to exist on this host.

is the same class of change that collapsed the old n4 ladder from 27..37 temps
to 8, so the rule applies to it first: re-derive before naming any rung.

**So the generator's defence survives a pass of exactly the class that

## BOTH staged pairs are SUPERSEDED: do not run them

gles2-core found a miscompile in the if-conversion join (`fce851e`): where only
one arm of an `if` writes a slot, the join selected from a register nothing had
written. It affects **30 of 137 sources** -- the FemtoVG fill/gradient/image/
stencil set Slint draws with.

Checked rather than assumed:

    fce851e ancestor of e81af25 ?  NO   (the lane-remap pair)
    fce851e ancestor of 4aa6087 ?  NO   (the load-snapshot pair)

So both pairs staged today emit wrong code for 30 sources, and their published
sha256s must not be run. They are kept in this document because their hashes
and predictions are still the honest record of what was staged and why; they are
not deleted, they are marked. The replacement is ONE pair from a `main` that
contains `f84d40d` + `4154f21` + `fce851e`, re-derived and re-published the same
way.

### The part that is mine: the suite did not catch it

`gl_test` scored 25/29 with the same four backend failures and 0 recoveries on
every online run today -- and every one of those runs was drawing with this
miscompile present. A suite that returns an unchanged score while 30 of 137
shaders compute from an unwritten register is not measuring what its score
implies.

The score was not wrong about what it tested; it is that none of the 29 cases
exercises the shape (`v = a; if (c) {} else { v = b; }` with both sides of the
condition checked). gles2-core is writing that case with pixel read-back, and it
joins the rung rather than being added quietly afterwards.

Worth stating plainly because it cuts against the reading I have been giving
all day: "no case moved" is evidence that nothing the suite covers regressed,
and it is not evidence that the compiler is correct. The wedge work has the same
shape -- a rung that draws says the GPU did not hang, not that the picture is
right -- and es100_vsprobe checks coverage and one pixel for exactly that
reason.

It was found by taking shaderc-remote's "40 vregs read but never written"
seriously as a correctness question instead of a curiosity, which is the second
time today a measurement someone nearly filed as noise turned out to be a
defect.
